chapters.title: Chapter 907. I Held Him Up Like A Trophy... And The Crowd Ate It Up
paragraphs: Rex’s head settled back into place with a slow, deliberate motion. A single droplet of blood trickled from the corner of his mouth where his teeth had pressed into his cheek, but his eyes remained glacial.
The momentary hope that had flickered in Theo’s shattered mind didn’t just die; it was incinerated.
Rex’s lips curled into something that wasn’t quite a smile. It was something far more predatory.
"My turn," Rex said.
The two words were quiet, but they carried the weight of a death sentence.
The shift in atmosphere was instantaneous. The casual mockery of the crowd vanished, replaced by a hungry, predatory tension.
They knew what was coming. They knew the mercy had expired.
Rex moved.
He didn’t charge; he exploded. Before Theo could even register the movement, Rex was inside his guard.
BAM!
A fist to the solar plexus folded Theo like parchment. The air left his lungs in a wet, strangled gurgle.
Before he could double over, Rex grabbed him by the throat and drove him backward into the stone pillar.
CRUNCH.
The impact reverberated through the hall as Theo’s spine collided with the ancient masonry.
"You wanted to play with fire, Prince?" Rex growled, his voice a guttural rasp.
WHAM.
A brutal uppercut caught Theo under the chin, snapping his head back so hard his teeth audibly collided.
CLACK.
"Then let’s see how you handle the furnace."
Rex unleashed a torrent of violence. This was no longer a demonstration; it was an execution of dignity.
Each strike was precise, devastating, and delivered with the intent to inflict maximum pain without the release of unconsciousness.
THUD. CRACK. WHACK.
A left hook to the ribs CRUNCH.
A spinning back kick to the kidney THUMP.
A series of rapid-fire jabs to the face that turned Theo’s features into a crimson mask.
"This is for your arrogance!" Rex roared as he drove a knee into Theo’s groin.
OOF.
"This is for your weakness!"
WHAM.
A hammer fist to the collarbone. "And this... this is for thinking you could ever be worthy of standing in my presence!"
Theo was no longer fighting back. He couldn’t.

He was a human punching bag, a broken vessel receiving the punishment he had earned. He could only flail weakly, his hands clawing uselessly at Rex’s armored forearms as he was systematically dismantled.
And then, something unexpected happened. The nobles, the very people who had been whispering in disgust, began to change.
The disgust turned into something darker. Something primal.
The cruelty of the scene tapped into something ancient and vicious within them. They weren’t cheering for the Nightwing heir; they were cheering for the spectacle of his destruction.
"Yes! Break him!" the Duke shouted, his face twisted in a grotesque grin.
"Show him what a real warrior looks like!" another bellowed, clapping his hands in time with Rex’s strikes.
CLAP. CLAP. CLAP.
"Crush the disgrace!" the crowd began to chant. "CRUSH THE DISGRACE! CRUSH THE DISGRACE!"
The chant grew louder, more feverish, feeding off Rex’s brutality. The training hall had transformed from a place of learning into a Roman colosseum.
The nobles were no longer observers; they were participants in Theo’s humiliation.
Rex seemed to feed off the energy. His strikes became faster and more vicious.
He grabbed Theo by his hair, forcing his head up to face the chanting crowd.
"Look at them, Theo!" Rex screamed over the roar of the spectators. "This is your kingdom now!"
"They don’t want a king! They want a victim!"
WHAM.
Rex drove a fist into Theo’s nose, sending blood spraying across the front row of the nobles. They didn’t flinch; they laughed.
"Look at the pretty prince bleeding for us!" someone shrieked with delight.
Theo’s eyes were rolled back in his head, his breathing nothing more than shallow, wet rattles. His magic had burned out, leaving him hollow and exposed.
Every time he tried to speak, more blood spilled from his lips.
"Please..." he wheezed, but the word was drowned out by the thunderous chant of the crowd.
Rex didn’t stop. He grabbed Theo by the belt and threw him across the floor like refuse.
SLIDE.
As Theo scrambled to find purchase on the slick stones, Rex descended upon him again.
BAM. BAM. BAM.
Three consecutive punches to the temple. Theo’s body convulsed, his limbs twitching spasmodically.
Rex stood over him, his shadow stretching long and monstrous across the broken boy.

"I’m not done ruining you, Theo," Rex whispered, though the crowd’s roar made it seem like he was shouting. "I’ll make sure that when you finally close your eyes for good, the last thing you see is the face of the man who proved you were nothing."
Rex raised both fists high above his head, the muscles in his shoulders coiling like serpents. The crowd went silent for one heartbeat of pure anticipation.
"DIE, YOU USELESS SHIT!" Rex bellowed.
BOOM.
Rex didn’t just want to hurt Theo; he wanted to erase him. The crowd’s bloodlust had become a tangible thing in the air, a poisonous fog that Rex inhaled to fuel his own cruelty.
Every time Rex’s fist connected with flesh, the hall erupted in a new wave of savage applause.
CRUNCH.
Rex drove a boot into Theo’s ribs, sending him tumbling sideways across the marble. The prince’s body hit a decorative pillar with a hollow THUD, leaving a smear of crimson on the white stone.
Before Theo could even attempt to draw breath, Rex was already there, his shadow falling over the broken boy like a shroud.
"You’re still breathing?" Rex asked, his voice dripping with mock disappointment. "After all that magic, after all that screaming?"
"You’re tougher than you look, little prince... Too bad toughness doesn’t make you competent."
WHAM.
Rex’s fist descended in a brutal hammer strike to Theo’s back.
OOF.
Theo’s face was pressed hard against the cold floor, his cheek grinding into the stone.
"Yes! Harder!" a baroness shrieked from the sidelines, her fan fluttering wildly. "Make him unrecognizable!"
"Break the Nightwing spine!" a knight roared, slamming his fist against his breastplate in approval.
CLANG. CLANG.
Rex grabbed Theo by the collar of his shredded tunic, hauling him upright just enough to deliver a series of devastating body blows.
THUD. THUD. THUD.
Each strike sounded like a butcher’s cleaver hitting meat. Theo’s legs flailed uselessly, his boots scraping against the floor as he struggled to maintain any semblance of balance.
"Look at him!" Rex shouted to the spectators, holding Theo aloft like a trophy of war. "This is your heir!"
"This is the future of the House of Nightwing!"
"A screaming, bleeding child who can’t even land a punch without begging for mercy!"
The humiliation was absolute. Theo wasn’t just losing a fight; he was being stripped of his humanity before the eyes of his entire world.
His eyes were swollen shut, his breathing was a series of wet, gurgling spasms, and his pride had been ground into the blood-soaked marble.
SMACK.
Rex delivered a stinging slap across Theo’s bloodied face, more for the insult than the damage. "Wake up, Prince... The show isn’t over until I say it’s over."
Rex pulled back his fist for what looked like the final, skull-crushing blow. The crowd’s chanting reached a deafening crescendo.
"CRUSH HIM! CRUSH HIM! CRUSH HIM!"
"ENOUGH!"
The command cut through the chaos like a blade through silk. The voice was cold, authoritative, and laced with an unmistakable tremor of restrained fury.
The hall fell silent instantly. Even the nobles froze mid-cheer. Rex paused, his fist cocked back, inches from Theo’s shattered face.
He turned his head slowly to see Aurelia walking down the center aisle. Her face was pale, her eyes fixed on the carnage, but her stride was steady.
She ignored Rex entirely as she approached the crumpled form on the floor. She knelt beside Theo, her expensive silk robes soaking up the blood pooling around him.
"Mother..." Theo’s voice was barely a whisper, a broken rasp that barely carried past her ear.
Without saying a word to Rex or the spectators, Aurelia reached down. Her movements were gentle, almost reverent, as she slipped one arm beneath his shoulders and the other behind his knees.
With surprising strength born of desperation, she began to help him up.
Theo’s body was limp, a sack of broken bones and bruised flesh. He didn’t resist; he couldn’t.
He allowed himself to be pulled upright, leaning heavily against her, his head lolling forward. His blood dripped steadily onto her pristine dress, but she didn’t seem to notice.
The silence in the hall was now different; it wasn’t the silence of anticipation but the uncomfortable silence of witnesses who had seen too much.
Aurelia steadied him, holding him upright as he struggled to find any semblance of equilibrium. Theo’s breathing was labored, each inhale a visible struggle against his broken ribs.
Slowly, painfully, he lifted his head. His one functional eye flickered open, blood streaming down his temple.
He didn’t cry. He didn’t scream. He didn’t curse.

He stood and looked at Rex with the specific flat expression of someone who has processed what has just happened and is currently in the specific state of someone deciding what to do with the processing.
"You know what you need to say to him now..." Aurelia said.

Rex pulled back his fist for what looked like the final, skull-crushing blow.
The crowd’s chanting reached a deafening crescendo.
"CRUSH HIM!
CRUSH HIM!
CRUSH HIM!"
"ENOUGH!"
The command cut through the chaos like a blade through silk.
The voice was cold, authoritative, and laced with an unmistakable tremor of restrained fury.
The hall fell silent instantly.
Even the nobles froze mid-cheer.
Rex paused, his fist cocked back, inches from Theo’s shattered face.
He turned his head slowly to see Aurelia walking down the center aisle.
Her face was pale, her eyes fixed on the carnage, but her stride was steady.
She ignored Rex entirely as she approached the crumpled form on the floor.
She knelt beside Theo, her expensive silk robes soaking up the blood pooling around him.
"Mother..." Theo’s voice was barely a whisper, a broken rasp that barely carried past her ear.
Without saying a word to Rex or the spectators, Aurelia reached down.
Her movements were gentle, almost reverent, as she slipped one arm beneath his shoulders and the other behind his knees.
With surprising strength born of desperation, she began to help him up.
Theo’s body was limp, a sack of broken bones and bruised flesh.
He didn’t resist; he couldn’t.
He allowed himself to be pulled upright, leaning heavily against her, his head lolling forward.
His blood dripped steadily onto her pristine dress, but she didn’t seem to notice.
The silence in the hall was now different; it wasn’t the silence of anticipation but the uncomfortable silence of witnesses who had seen too much.
Aurelia steadied him, holding him upright as he struggled to find any semblance of equilibrium.
Theo’s breathing was labored, each inhale a visible struggle against his broken ribs.
Slowly, painfully, he lifted his head.
His one functional eye flickered open, blood streaming down his temple.
He didn’t cry.
He didn’t scream.
He didn’t curse.

He stood and looked at Rex with the specific flat expression of someone who has processed what has just happened and is currently in the specific state of someone deciding what to do with the processing.
"You know what you need to say to him now..." Aurelia said.

chapters.title: Chapter 908. The Trap Sprang Exactly As Designed, No Luck Involved
paragraphs: The air in the training hall didn’t just feel still after Aurelia’s intervention; it felt vacuum-sealed, as if the very oxygen had been sucked out by the sheer force of the humiliation that had just transpired.
The metallic tang of blood—Theo’s blood—hung heavy in the nostrils of every noble present, mixing with the sharp, acrid sting of spent magical energy.

Theo leaned into Aurelia, his body a ruined marionette of shattered cartilage and torn muscle. His ribs felt like jagged glass grinding against his lungs with every shallow gasp, and his vision was a kaleidoscopic smear of crimson and gray.
Inside his mind, there was no screaming. There was no weeping. There was only a terrifying, glacial quiet, the sound of a furnace cooling after a catastrophic meltdown.
The rage had burned itself out, leaving behind something harder, something colder, and something infinitely more dangerous than mere anger.
He steadied himself, forcing his broken limbs to obey. He peeled himself away from Aurelia’s supporting arm, swaying momentarily before finding his footing.

His face was a grotesque mask: one eye swollen into a purple slit, his nose crooked and weeping blood, and his lips split to the point of exposing raw nerves. But his eyes, those eyes were horrifying.

He stood and looked at Rex with the specific flat expression of someone who has processed what has just happened and is currently in the specific state of someone deciding what to do with the processing.
He wasn’t looking at a rival. He was looking at a variable that needed to be corrected.
"The position is yours," Theo said. His voice was startling devoid of the hysterical cracking from moments before.
It was level, hollow, and utterly devoid of inflection. It was the voice of a dead man speaking from the bottom of a well.
Whatever was simmering beneath that calm was not visible to the naked eye, but it radiated off him like heat from a tombstone.
Without waiting for a rebuttal, without acknowledging the blood-soaked nobles or the mercenary who had just dismantled his dignity, Theo turned.

Each step was a calculated agony, his boots squelching wetly in the pooling blood as he walked off the floor. His gait was stiff, mechanical, the movement of a man who had severed his connection to pain in order to survive the walk.

Aurelia watched him go, her pale features unreadable, though her hands trembled slightly where they were hidden beneath her sleeves. She waited until the echoes of Theo’s retreating footsteps died down before she turned her attention to the room.
The predator had been replaced by the matriarch.
She looked at Rex, her gaze sharp enough to draw blood.
"Rex Rexilion," she announced.

Her voice rang through the hall, formal and absolute, carrying the crushing weight of a household head speaking to her domain. "By the authority vested in me during the absence of the primary authority, you are hereby appointed as the acting combat director for the Nightwing unit training program until their return."

The twelve elite fighters standing in the periphery didn’t hesitate. In unison, they performed the formal acknowledgment, a synchronized strike of palms against breastplates that sounded like a single, thunderous heartbeat.
CLANG.
The sound reverberated off the vaulted ceilings, sealing the decree.

Rex stood in the center of the training hall. Beneath his calm exterior, he felt a surge of something primal: the deep, cold satisfaction of a predator whose trap had not only sprung but had been sprung exactly as designed.
This wasn’t luck. This was the exquisite precision of a plan executing at the level it was intended to, the clean, mathematical quality of sustained work finally yielding its inevitable result.
He did not show it. His face remained a neutral canvas.

Instead, he offered Aurelia a bow, a controlled gesture that conveyed warm, slightly surprised gratitude. He played the role of the honored subordinate perfectly, masking the fact that he had just orchestrated the systematic psychological annihilation of the House’s heir.
Hours later, the hall had surrendered to the evening shadows. The spectacle was over.

Iris had departed to seek sustenance; Diana and Elaris remained in low conversation near the entrance like distant ghosts, and Aurelia was occupied with the grim task of debriefing her standard setters.
Rex stood alone in the dead center of the training hall. The silence here was different now; it was heavy with the memory of screams and the phantom pain of broken bones.
He closed his eyes and summoned the only truth that mattered.
The system interface flickered to life before his mind’s eye, glowing with a cold, ethereal light.

He navigated past the trivialities, past the combat techniques and elemental augmentations, straight to the forbidden architecture of his ambition. He moved toward the section he had been constructing since the blood-soaked fields of Lustia’s domain, the capability that would transform him from a mere combatant into something that could rewrite the fundamental laws of existence.
He found it. The text didn’t just appear; it burned into his consciousness.
[SOUL MANIPULATION FULL POTENTIAL]
[COMPLETE OPERATION WITHIN THE SOUL REGISTER OF BIOLOGICAL ENTITIES.]

[ENABLES: READING THE SOUL’S CURRENT STATE AND RECENT HISTORY; COMMUNICATION WITH RECENTLY DEPARTED SOULS WITHIN THE TEMPORAL WINDOW OF THEIR TRANSITION; TEMPORARY ANCHORING OF A DEPARTING SOUL TO THE PHYSICAL TIMELINE; MODIFICATION OF SOUL LAYER BINDINGS, INCLUDING DESIGNATION TIES AND DESIRE BONDS; AND DETECTION OF SOUL-LEVEL WORKINGS APPLIED BY EXTERNAL FORCES.]

[COMMUNICATION WINDOW FOR DEPARTED SOULS: APPROXIMATELY 30 DAYS FROM THE DATE OF DEPARTURE. AT FULL POTENTIAL, BEYOND THIS WINDOW, SOULS HAVE COMPLETED THEIR TRANSITION AND ARE NO LONGER ACCESSIBLE THROUGH THIS SKILL.]
[ANCHORING FUNCTION: TEMPORARILY PREVENTS SOUL DEPARTURE FOR UP TO 72 HOURS, ALLOWING EXTENDED COMMUNICATION OR STABILIZATION OF CRITICALLY INJURED TARGETS.]
[MODIFICATION FUNCTION: CAN ADD, ALTER, OR REMOVE SOUL LAYER BINDINGS, INCLUDING APOSTLE DESIGNATIONS, DESIRE BOND EFFECTS, AND TEMPORAL ANCHORING WORKINGS APPLIED BY EXTERNAL ENTITIES.]
[COST: 11,200 POINTS]
Rex stared at the number. It was a king’s ransom in energy. His fingers invisible to the physical world hovered over the selection.
His mind flashed to the plans with Iris, to the complex web of loyalties and divine designations he needed to unravel. This was the scalpel he needed to dissect destiny itself.
[Current Energy Balance: 13,150 points]
There was no hesitation. No doubt.
Only the cold calculation of a man who had already decided what kind of god he would become.
He selected it.
[PURCHASE CONFIRMED.]
[SOUL MANIPULATION FULL POTENTIAL HAS BEEN INTEGRATED INTO THE USER’S SOUL REGISTER.]
[Current Energy Balance: 1,950 points]

The integration arrived differently from every other skill integration he had experienced because the soul register was not a register that any of his previous integrations had accessed. The closest analogue was the Emotional Insight’s passive read, which touched the emotional surface of the people around him.
Soul manipulation went deeper than that, below the emotional surface into the specific layer where the things that made a person a person rather than a body were located.
He stood in the training hall and felt the world change texture.
Not dramatically. The floor was still the same.

The hall’s ambient sounds were still the same. But the people in it now had a depth that they had not had thirty seconds ago—not the acquisition of strength for its own sake, but a visible extension below the physical and energetic registers into the specific quality of whatever it was that made each of them the specific person they were.

Aurelia’s soul signature was the specific quality of a person who had built her identity around the cultivation of strength, not the acquisition of strength for its own sake but the specific commitment to being capable enough to protect the things she valued.
It had the warmth of someone who had been doing this for decades and had found it genuinely sustaining.
Iris’s soul signature had the flat, sharp quality of someone in acute grief who had not yet reached the stage of integrating that grief. The fresh quality of loss was still actively affecting her.

Rex felt the Veylor connection through Iris’s soul register without looking for it, the specific soul-layer bond that a genuine relationship left even after one of the parties had departed, a thread that ran from Iris’s present state into the direction that recent departures went.
The thread was there.
It was approximately thirty-six hours old.
It was accessible.
Rex filed this with the flat satisfaction of confirmed intelligence and closed the skill catalog.
He looked at the empty training hall.

He looked at the number in his energy balance, which was 1,950 points remaining after the Soul Manipulation purchase, and he considered the specific constraints that this number imposed on his operational options in the near term.
He was not concerned.
He was in the Nightwing household.
He had a month.
He looked at the training hall’s ceiling, the high stone arch that the Nightwing family had built specifically for a space where the ceiling did not need to limit what was done beneath it.
"Let the one month of fun," Rex said, to the ceiling, in the flat, private register of someone speaking to themselves with complete honesty, "begin."

He walked out of the training hall into the rear courtyard of the Nightwing household, where the morning light was now bright, the grey sky replaced by the distinct quality of a day that had chosen to be itself, and Rex moved through it with the ease of someone who knows exactly where they are going and is in no particular hurry to get there.
He was, after all, the acting combat director of the Nightwing household’s training program.
He had things to teach.

chapters.title: Chapter 909. I Read The Room Like A Forge Instead Of A Battlefield Today
paragraphs: The atmosphere in the training hall on the second morning carried a different charge than the day before, a charged, static tension that made the fine hairs on Rex’s arms stand on end. Yesterday had been an explosion of violence; today was the uncomfortable, suffocating aftermath.

Word had spread through the Nightwing household overnight with the insidious speed of a plague. It didn’t travel through official channels or formal decrees; it moved through the whispered conversations of chambermaids polishing silver, the knowing glances exchanged between armored guards in the corridors, and the hushed tones of servants passing trays.
By the time Rex arrived at the sixth hour, the hall was already unnaturally crowded.

The twelve elite fighters were no longer the sole occupants of the floor. Junior guards, whose duty called them elsewhere, had suddenly discovered a desperate need to practice their footwork in this specific hall.

Two administrative staff members had positioned themselves near the arched entrance with the transparent excuse of delivering urgent messages—messages that Rex knew intimately could have waited until sunset. Even the hangers-on, distant cousins, and in-laws who typically avoided anything that involved genuine exertion or sweat had slunk into the shadows along the walls, their eyes sharp with morbid curiosity.
They weren’t here for training. They were here to witness the aftermath of a spectacle.
They wanted to see if the demon who had systematically dismantled the heir was real or if yesterday had been some fever dream of blood and broken bones.
Aurelia noticed the gathering. Her lips pressed into a thin, firm line, but she made no move to disperse them.
Rex understood this silence as a concession; she was allowing them their morbid fascination, as long as it didn’t interfere with the lesson.
"They want to see if yesterday was real," Aurelia said quietly as they crossed the polished stone floor together.
Her voice was low enough that only Rex could hear, but it carried the weary authority of a woman who had spent the night managing both physical injuries and political fallout. "I told them it was."
"They did not fully believe me until they saw the twelve limping through breakfast this morning."

Rex’s expression remained impassive, though his mind briefly cataloged the memory of the previous day: the wet crunch of ribs under his boot, the way Theo’s nose had given way under his fist, the crimson spray that had painted the floor.
"I did not leave anyone limping badly enough to matter," Rex countered.
"You left Rilena favoring her left ankle," Aurelia corrected, though there was no venom in her tone. "It is not a complaint..."
"She earned that injury honestly, and she has already told me twice this morning that she wants to run the sequence again as soon as the ache subsides."
"That is what a good result looks like in this household, Rex."
"Pain that produces determination instead of resentment. And pain that makes them hungry rather than broken."
Rex nodded grimly. That was the core of his philosophy: violence as a tool for refinement, not merely destruction.
As they approached the center of the hall, Rex spotted Diana. She was already on the floor, moving through a series of fluid, lethal stretches.

She was dressed in practical training gear designed to move as an extension of her own body, revealing the corded muscle and lean grace that made her such a formidable asset. When she sensed his approach, she caught his eye across the space.
Her gaze held that particular expression she had cultivated over the months, a look that wasn’t quite a smile but held the unspoken promise of one if he proved himself worthy of the effort.
"You are late," Diana called out as he closed the distance.

Her voice was clear, carrying across the silent hall, drawing the attention of the spectators in the shadows. It was a blatant lie, but it was the specific kind of playful falsehood Diana used as an opening rather than a reprimand.
Rex stopped at the designated training mark, his stance relaxed but his presence commanding.
"I am exactly on time," he replied smoothly. "You simply arrived early because you wanted a front-row seat to my warm-up."
Diana’s lips quirked upward.
"I arrived early because Aurelia asked me to help demonstrate the morning drills," she said, but the slight tremor in her voice and the way the corner of her mouth twitched betrayed her.
The first reason hadn’t been entirely false, but it certainly wasn’t the only one.
Aurelia raised her hands and delivered a single, sharp clap. The sound was not merely a noise; it was an auditory command that reverberated off the vaulted stone ceilings like a crack of thunder.

In an instant, the loose, murmuring crowd along the walls stiffened. The casual posture of the junior guards vanished, replaced by the rigid alertness of soldiers who knew that when a Nightwing matriarch spoke, the world tended to stop turning.
"Today is different from yesterday," Aurelia said, her voice cutting through the remaining silence like a honed blade. "Yesterday was a demonstration of capability."
A pause followed, heavy with the memory of the previous day’s violence.

"Today is instruction." Her gaze swept across the room, pausing briefly on the spectators before locking onto the twelve elite fighters. "Rex Rexilion holds the acting director’s authority in this hall until Leonidas returns."
"Every person standing on this floor is to treat his corrections with the same reverence you would afford mine."

Her eyes shifted to the periphery, narrowing as they landed on the extended family members and the administrative staff who had lingered too long. "That includes the family members who wandered in to watch."
"If you intend to sit against that wall, you will sit in absolute silence."
"If you cannot respect the sanctity of this training hall, you will be put to work. And I promise you, the labor I assign will be far less pleasant than watching."
One of the cousins, a young man who had been leaning smugly against a pillar, bolted upright, his face flushing crimson as he scrambled to find a more unobtrusive position.
Rex began to move. He paced the floor with the same deliberate, predatory economy he had shown the day before, but his internal focus had shifted.
Yesterday, he had been reading the room as a battlefield, evaluating exits, measuring distances, and assessing threats.
Today, he was reading the room like a forge. He wasn’t looking at the floor; he was looking through the people.

He saw the twelve elites: they were bruised, yes, but their eyes held something more dangerous than pain. They held the raw, unvarnished hunger of those who had been broken and had decided they would never be broken again.
He saw the junior guards: a patchwork of potential and dangerous inconsistency, their stances revealing the sloppy habits that inexperience breeds.
He saw Diana: a blade already sharp, but one that needed the careful whetstone of refinement to reach a level of lethality the House of Nightwing had not witnessed in generations.
And then, there was Theo.

Near the back of the formation, standing like a specter in the shadows, was the heir. His arms were crossed tightly over his chest, his face still bearing the faint, yellowish bruises of yesterday’s assault.

He was watching Rex with that same unnerving, flat expression, the expression of a man who was not frustrated but who was calculating. Rex noted his position, the silent challenge in the boy’s stare, and deliberately said nothing. To acknowledge the provocation would be to grant it power.
"We start with the fundamentals," Rex announced, his voice carrying to every corner of the hall. "Not because any of you lack them."
"But because fundamentals are the first things to erode when the blood starts flowing and the lungs begin to burn."
"I would rather find your flaws here, in the controlled safety of this hall, than find them in a real engagement where erosion costs you your life or the lives of those beside you."
The lesson began with brutal honesty. Rex moved through the space like a ghost of discipline.
He demonstrated the perfect stance: the precise distribution of weight that allowed for instantaneous redirection, the subtle angle of the hips that turned a defensive posture into a coiled spring.

He moved from person to person, his touch clinical and uncompromising. He would step behind a junior guard, his hand applying firm, corrective pressure to an elbow that was turned half an inch too far outward.
"Your balance is compromised," Rex would murmur, his voice quiet but carrying the weight of absolute truth. "Fix it, or you’ll be dead before you can draw your sword."
He moved to another, adjusting the angle of a shoulder. "Stop watching their hands."
"The hands lie. Watch their hips, their eyes, and their breathing."
"The body cannot hide its intent."

The air in the hall grew thick with effort. There was no shouting, no grand speeches, only the rhythmic sound of breathing, the occasional scrape of boots on stone, and the quiet, deadly precision of Rex Rexilion systematically rebuilding the unit from the bone up.

Rex nodded grimly.
That was the core of his philosophy: violence as a tool for refinement, not merely destruction.
As they approached the center of the hall, Rex spotted Diana.
She was already on the floor, moving through a series of fluid, lethal stretches.
She was dressed in practical training gear designed to move as an extension of her own body, revealing the corded muscle and lean grace that made her such a formidable asset.
When she sensed his approach, she caught his eye across the space.
Her gaze held that particular expression she had cultivated over the months, a look that wasn’t quite a smile but held the unspoken promise of one if he proved himself worthy of the effort.
"You are late," Diana called out as he closed the distance.
Her voice was clear, carrying across the silent hall, drawing the attention of the spectators in the shadows.
It was a blatant lie, but it was the specific kind of playful falsehood Diana used as an opening rather than a reprimand.
Rex stopped at the designated training mark, his stance relaxed but his presence commanding.
"I am exactly on time," he replied smoothly.
"You simply arrived early because you wanted a front-row seat to my warm-up."
Diana’s lips quirked upward.
"I arrived early because Aurelia asked me to help demonstrate the morning drills," she said, but the slight tremor in her voice and the way the corner of her mouth twitched betrayed her.
The first reason hadn’t been entirely false, but it certainly wasn’t the only one.
Aurelia raised her hands and delivered a single, sharp clap.
The sound was not merely a noise; it was an auditory command that reverberated off the vaulted stone ceilings like a crack of thunder.
In an instant, the loose, murmuring crowd along the walls stiffened.
The casual posture of the junior guards vanished, replaced by the rigid alertness of soldiers who knew that when a Nightwing matriarch spoke, the world tended to stop turning.
"Today is different from yesterday," Aurelia said, her voice cutting through the remaining silence like a honed blade.
"Yesterday was a demonstration of capability."
A pause followed, heavy with the memory of the previous day’s violence.
"Today is instruction." Her gaze swept across the room, pausing briefly on the spectators before locking onto the twelve elite fighters.
"Rex Rexilion holds the acting director’s authority in this hall until Leonidas returns."
"Every person standing on this floor is to treat his corrections with the same reverence you would afford mine."
Her eyes shifted to the periphery, narrowing as they landed on the extended family members and the administrative staff who had lingered too long.
"That includes the family members who wandered in to watch."
"If you intend to sit against that wall, you will sit in absolute silence."
"If you cannot respect the sanctity of this training hall, you will be put to work.
And I promise you, the labor I assign will be far less pleasant than watching."
One of the cousins, a young man who had been leaning smugly against a pillar, bolted upright, his face flushing crimson as he scrambled to find a more unobtrusive position.
Rex began to move.
He paced the floor with the same deliberate, predatory economy he had shown the day before, but his internal focus had shifted.
Yesterday, he had been reading the room as a battlefield, evaluating exits, measuring distances, and assessing threats.
Today, he was reading the room like a forge.
He wasn’t looking at the floor; he was looking through the people.
He saw the twelve elites: they were bruised, yes, but their eyes held something more dangerous than pain.
They held the raw, unvarnished hunger of those who had been broken and had decided they would never be broken again.
He saw the junior guards: a patchwork of potential and dangerous inconsistency, their stances revealing the sloppy habits that inexperience breeds.
He saw Diana: a blade already sharp, but one that needed the careful whetstone of refinement to reach a level of lethality the House of Nightwing had not witnessed in generations.
And then, there was Theo.
Near the back of the formation, standing like a specter in the shadows, was the heir.
His arms were crossed tightly over his chest, his face still bearing the faint, yellowish bruises of yesterday’s assault.
He was watching Rex with that same unnerving, flat expression, the expression of a man who was not frustrated but who was calculating.
Rex noted his position, the silent challenge in the boy’s stare, and deliberately said nothing.
To acknowledge the provocation would be to grant it power.
"We start with the fundamentals," Rex announced, his voice carrying to every corner of the hall.
"Not because any of you lack them."
"But because fundamentals are the first things to erode when the blood starts flowing and the lungs begin to burn."
"I would rather find your flaws here, in the controlled safety of this hall, than find them in a real engagement where erosion costs you your life or the lives of those beside you."
The lesson began with brutal honesty.
Rex moved through the space like a ghost of discipline.
He demonstrated the perfect stance: the precise distribution of weight that allowed for instantaneous redirection, the subtle angle of the hips that turned a defensive posture into a coiled spring.
He moved from person to person, his touch clinical and uncompromising.
He would step behind a junior guard, his hand applying firm, corrective pressure to an elbow that was turned half an inch too far outward.
"Your balance is compromised," Rex would murmur, his voice quiet but carrying the weight of absolute truth.
"Fix it, or you’ll be dead before you can draw your sword."
He moved to another, adjusting the angle of a shoulder.
"Stop watching their hands."
"The hands lie.
Watch their hips, their eyes, and their breathing."
"The body cannot hide its intent."
The air in the hall grew thick with effort.

There was no shouting, no grand speeches, only the rhythmic sound of breathing, the occasional scrape of boots on stone, and the quiet, deadly precision of Rex Rexilion systematically rebuilding the unit from the bone up.

chapters.title: Chapter 910. I Kissed Her In Front Of Everyone, And Then... The Room Ceased To Exist
paragraphs: Rex saved Diana for last. It was a calculated move, a deliberate choice that served both his training regimen and the unspoken power dynamics simmering beneath the surface of the hall.
"Your stance is already correct," he announced, his voice carrying across the room with clear authority.

He wanted the spectators, the curious cousins, and the nervous junior guards to hear it. He wanted them to understand that ’correct’ was not some abstract concept reserved for legends; it was a tangible reality that could be achieved through sweat and discipline.

Then, he stepped closer, lowering his voice until it was a private murmur meant only for her ears, cutting through the ambient noise of the hall. "But your weight shifts a fraction too early when you commit to a strike."
"You’re telegraphing your intent before your muscles even contract... It has been costing you precious milliseconds of speed for as long as I have watched you fight."
Diana didn’t flinch, and she didn’t deflect with a quip. Her eyes locked onto his, burning with a focused intensity.
"Show me," she commanded.
Rex moved behind her. He positioned himself close enough that his presence was undeniable, close enough that the heat from his body could be felt, but he maintained a clinical detachment.
This was not an invitation to intimacy; it was a demonstration of mechanics. He placed his hand firmly at her hip, his fingers finding the exact point of tension where her balance wavered.
"Wait for the coil," he whispered, his breath ghosting near her ear. "Don’t lean into the strike."
"Let the strike come from the floor."

He guided her through the motion, physically forcing her body to delay the shift by a heartbeat. He felt the micro adjustments in her muscles as she resisted the old habit, the way her core tightened to compensate.
When she finally executed the movement, the correction was instinctive.
"There," he said, withdrawing his hand. "That is the difference between a strike that lands and a strike that kills."
Diana launched the strike again, alone this time. The difference was visceral.

Even to the untrained eyes of the household staff watching from the sidelines, there was a new, lethal quality to her movement. There was an added snap, a whip crack of energy, that came from the weight arriving at the exact microsecond the force required it, rather than bleeding off prematurely.
"That is going to matter," Diana murmured, more to herself than to him.
Her jaw was set, her mind already cataloging the adjustment as a permanent part of her arsenal.

From the shadows at the rear of the hall, Rex could feel Theo’s gaze like a physical weight. The heir was watching the exchange with an expression that was performing the exhausting labor of appearing professionally interested, but he was failing.
Beneath the mask of neutrality, Rex could sense the corrosive burn of resentment and the dangerous calculation of a wounded predator watching a rival claim territory.
The morning dissolved into the familiar, brutal rhythm of the training hall. Rex circulated through paired sparring sessions like a surgeon moving between patients.

He watched Iris as she was paired with a nervous junior guard; she demonstrated a rare, unspoken grace, dialing back her lethal intensity just enough to allow the boy to learn without being maimed, all while maintaining the razor-sharp quality of her technique.

He intervened twice during a session between two of the twelve elites, stopping them mid-swing because their footwork, while technically flawless, was tactically lazy; they were fighting like athletes, not survivors.

He allowed Aurelia to conduct her own segment without interference. There was no need for his critique there; she was a force of nature in her own right, and both of them understood that his role today was to observe, not to usurp.
As she worked, Rex remained a silent sentinel, his mind working like a ledger, cataloguing who was truly evolving and who was merely coasting on the reputation they had earned yesterday.
Finally, the time came for the closing ritual. Rex stepped into the center of the circle and gestured to Diana.

The unspoken understanding between them hung heavy in the air, a tension so palpable that several of the onlookers instinctively took a half step back. No one questioned it; in this house, competence was the only currency that mattered, and the chemistry between them was irrelevant compared to the lethal potential they shared.
"Full intensity," Rex said, his voice dropping into a register that signaled the end of instruction and the beginning of combat. "Do not expect me to hold back."
"I would rather you discover the true ceiling of your capabilities now than find out in the middle of a slaughter when you realize you’ve been training against an artificially soft version of me."
Diana’s lips curled into a genuine, dangerous smile, the smile of a wolf recognizing another.
"Good," she said, rolling her shoulders as she settled into a deadly crouch. "I was going to ask anyway."

Diana was transformed. It wasn’t that a single morning of technical adjustment had rewritten her entire combat identity—that would be impossible—but she possessed the rare, terrifying quality of a predator who could absorb a lesson and weaponize it instantly.
Most fighters required hours, sometimes days, to translate verbal correction into instinctive muscle memory. Diana did it in heartbeats.
Her weight shift was no longer a tell; it was a coiled spring. Her recovery between exchanges was seamless, her movements stripped of any wasted motion that might betray her next intent.
She pressed him harder than she ever had before. Every strike carried more conviction and venom.

She wasn’t just sparring; she was testing the limits of the new reality Rex had handed her. Rex allowed the engagement to stretch, letting the intensity climb until the air in the hall felt charged with static.
Watching her evolve in real time provided a grim satisfaction that bypassed his tactical mind entirely; it was the raw appreciation of a craftsman watching steel become unbreakable.
The climax of the exchange came with brutal efficiency. Diana launched a desperate, high-velocity strike aimed at his throat, a move that would have been fatal in any other context.
Rex didn’t flinch. He stepped inside the arc of her arm, his movement a blur of controlled violence.
He caught her wrist, pivoted his hips, and used her own momentum against her. With a precise, controlled application of force, he redirected her trajectory into a guided fall.
There was a sharp thud as her back hit the mats, but she absorbed the impact with the fluid grace he had drilled into her, rolling to dissipate the energy rather than fighting it.

The hall fell into a suffocating silence. It was the kind of quiet that occurs when witnesses realize they are watching something primal, something that defies the polite vocabulary of training and enters the realm of something far more dangerous.
Diana lay on the floor for a heartbeat, chest heaving, sweat slicking her skin. Then, she looked up at him and grinned.
It was an unguarded, feral expression, one she never permitted herself when the household’s eyes were upon her.
"Better...?" she panted, the word punctuated by her ragged breathing.
"Much better," Rex replied, his voice carrying an unfamiliar note of genuine approval.
He reached down, offering his hand.

When she took it, he didn’t simply pull her up; he hauled her close, the motion deliberately violating the distance expected between instructor and student. For several seconds, the hundreds of eyes watching them—the guards, the servants, the scheming cousins—simply ceased to exist.
Rex looked down at her flushed face, her pupils dilated with exertion and something else, and felt something that had absolutely nothing to do with strategy, training, or control.
"You are doing that thing," Diana whispered, her voice low enough to be private despite the silence of the hall. "That thing where you look at me like I am the only person in the room."
"You are... currently," Rex said, his gaze unblinking, holding hers with an intensity that felt like a physical claim. "The room will still be here in a minute, but this moment will not."
Then, he kissed her. It was not a tentative gesture; it was unhurried, possessive, and utterly defiant of the audience surrounding them.
In front of the entire training hall, Rex Rexilion claimed her. Diana didn’t recoil; she didn’t hesitate.
Her hand came up to rest against his chest, fingers splaying over his heartbeat, not to push him away but to anchor herself to him.

Across the hall, Aurelia remained motionless, but the corners of her mouth lifted in a small, knowing smile, the approval of a matriarch who understood that power was often forged in the heat of passion as much as in battle.

Elaris, watching from the sidelines, pressed a hand to her mouth to stifle a delighted gasp. Iris offered a brief, warm smile of amusement before returning to the solitary work of stretching out her bruised shoulder.
Only one person refused to witness it. Theo turned his head away first, his jaw working silently, his eyes fixed on the far wall as he retreated into the bitter shadows of his own resentment.

chapters.title: Chapter 911. He Grabbed A Towel Like It Was A Personality
paragraphs: Theo had been watching. He had been watching since the first bell of the sixth hour, a silent specter at the periphery of the training hall.

He had constructed a fortress of rationalizations to protect himself from the truth: that he was watching with the obsessive focus of a man who had been usurped. He told himself it was professional duty that a Nightwing heir must closely monitor the methods of the acting director.
He told himself he was studying Rex’s techniques to better understand the threat. He told himself he was simply assessing the new power dynamic of the household.
Each lie was thinner than the last, crumbling under the weight of the undeniable reality unfolding before him.

When the kiss ended and the hall began to fracture back into its normal rhythms, Theo moved. He crossed the stone floor without conscious intent, his boots making no sound, drawn by a gravitational pull he couldn’t resist.
He found himself standing near the wall where Diana had left her belongings. His hand reached out, almost involuntarily, and gripped the rough fabric of her towel.
It was a pathetic, automatic gesture, the action of a man whose hands needed a purpose because his mind was drowning in something he refused to name.
Diana was still standing near Rex, her chest still rising and falling from the exertion, when she sensed his approach. She turned, wiping sweat from her brow, and her expression shifted instantly.
The warmth she had shown Rex vanished, replaced by the polished, impenetrable neutrality of a trained operative.
"Thank you," she said, reaching for the towel.
Her voice was flat, stripped of inflection, carrying nothing but the hollow courtesy she would extend to a stranger.
Theo didn’t retreat.
"You have improved," he said, his voice carrying a strained edge that he couldn’t quite suppress. "Since yesterday... the change is... not subtle."
"He is a good teacher," Diana replied.

She didn’t look at him. She began wiping the salt from her neck, her body language already angling away from him in the precise, dismissive posture of someone who had already decided that this interaction was a tactical waste of time.
"I could see that," Theo said, his jaw tightening.

He stood there for a moment, the silence between them stretching uncomfortably long, filled only by the distant sounds of other fighters resuming their drills. Then, driven by some desperate, ill-advised impulse, the kind that makes men ruin themselves, he pushed further.
"We used to spar together... before all of this and before the House became... this. You remember."
Diana paused mid-motion. For a heartbeat, something flickered behind her eyes, a ghost of a memory, but it was gone before it could take root.
"I remember," she said coldly. "We were fifteen..."
"You broke my wrist because you didn’t know how to control your own momentum, and I forgave you because we were children who knew nothing of consequence."
The memory hung between them like a blade. Theo flinched almost imperceptibly at the reminder of his own past weakness, his fingers curling tighter around the towel.

"I have thought about that sometimes," Theo said, his voice dropping to something raw and almost vulnerable, though it still tasted of bitter regret. "I’ve thought about how different everything might have been."
"How different we might have been if we had kept training together instead of drifting into separate circles."
Diana finally turned to face him fully. The mask of polite neutrality didn’t just slip; it shattered.
The patience she had been extending that fragile, customary courtesy withered and died in her eyes.
"Theo," she said.

Her voice wasn’t loud, but it possessed a terrifying, razor-edged clarity that seemed to suck the air out of the immediate space around them. "I am going to say this once, and I am going to say it clearly, because I think you are trapped in some delusion that if you say enough small things in enough quiet moments, something will eventually land differently than the last one did."
"You think you’re planting seeds... You’re not."
Theo opened his mouth to speak, but she cut through him like a blade through silk.
"It will not happen... I am not drifting back toward you."
"There is no version of the last several months, no timeline, no alternative reality where that happens."
"I did not choose Rex because you were unavailable, or because the timing was wrong, or because I was looking for an escape."

"I chose him because I love him... plainly, violently, and with a certainty I have never felt for anyone else." Her gaze hardened, becoming something cold and unforgiving. "And every time you find some pathetic excuse to stand near me and invoke memories from when we were fifteen, it doesn’t make me nostalgic, Theo."
"It doesn’t make me remember a lost connection... It makes me uncomfortable and it makes me want to walk away from you."
Theo’s jaw tightened so hard the muscles along his temple visibly pulsed. His hands clenched into fists at his sides, the knuckles whitening.
The humiliation was visible in the way his shoulders tensed, a predator caught in a trap of his own making.
"I was not trying to make you uncomfortable," he said, his voice strangled, defensive, and dangerously thin.
"I know you weren’t trying to," Diana said. Her expression shifted then.
The anger ebbed away, leaving behind something far more devastating: pity. It was a soft, hollow sound in her voice that cut deeper than any insult. "That is actually the worst part of this, Theo."
’You aren’t doing this maliciously... You don’t even realize you’re doing it."
"Which means you don’t know how to stop, which means this cycle will continue until you finally develop the spine to actually let me go..."
"I cannot make that decision for you, and I cannot grieve the ghost of our childhood for you."
She didn’t wait for his rebuttal. She didn’t give him the satisfaction of watching him break.
She simply turned her back on him, a dismissal more absolute than any physical blow, and walked back toward the center of the training floor.

Her destination was Rex. He was standing there, framed by the afternoon light filtering through the high windows, engaged in a low-voiced conversation with Aurelia about the afternoon’s tactical schedule.

He hadn’t moved, hadn’t flinched, and hadn’t broken eye contact with the matriarch, but Rex was not a man who missed details. He had heard every syllable of the exchange, every inflection of Diana’s pain and Theo’s desperation, yet he remained as impassive as carved granite.
Theo remained frozen at the wall. His fingers curled reflexively around the empty air where the towel had been, his hand grasping at nothing.
He stood there, a disgraced prince in his own kingdom, watching the woman he wanted walk toward the man who had already won.

The training session dragged on for another hour, stretching long past the point where most of the observers had drifted away to their respective obligations. The hall gradually emptied, the echoing shouts and the rhythmic clatter of weapons fading until the space held only those with a genuine reason or obsession to remain.
Aurelia moved through the remaining crowd like a queen surveying her domain, dismissing the last of the junior guards with crisp, unyielding instructions for the afternoon’s duties.
Iris departed with a subtle alertness in her step, leaving to investigate something at the household’s outer perimeter that had been gnawing at her assassin instincts since sunrise.
Elaris left last, carrying the unmistakable, buoyant energy of someone who had gained far more entertainment from watching the morning’s drama than she had anticipated.

Rex remained. He began a final, solitary drill, the kind of brutal, punishing conditioning work that Martial Arts Mastery did not strictly require for combat efficiency but that his body demanded for survival.

It was the raw discipline of maintaining the foundation upon which his lethal abilities rested. His movements were mechanical yet explosive; he moved through shadow boxing sequences that looked more like controlled strikes against invisible throats, followed by explosive bursts of footwork that left scuff marks on the stone.

By the time he finally ceased, the hall felt cavernous and still. His shirt was soaked through, clinging to the hard planes of his chest like a second skin, and his breathing came in deep, ragged draws.
This was not the performed exhaustion of a demonstration; it was the honest, bone-deep fatigue of a body that had been pushed to its absolute limit for three consecutive hours.
Diana was already there, waiting at the edge of the floor. She didn’t greet him with words; she simply existed there, a steady presence in the quiet hall.

As he approached, she handed him a cup of water. He took it without ceremony, drinking half of it in desperate, greedy gulps, feeling the cold liquid cut through the furnace of his throat. When he finished, she took the empty cup and reached for a fresh towel.
"Sit," she commanded. Her voice was quiet, but it carried the weight of an order he wouldn’t or couldn’t refuse. "You have been standing since before dawn, Rex."
"I am fine," he said.

The words were true; his body was built for this, forged in fires far hotter than a morning drill, but he knew it wasn’t the point. He could see it in the way her jaw set, the way her eyes traced the tension in his shoulders.
Diana’s expression didn’t waver. She didn’t argue, because she didn’t need to.
She simply stared at him with that terrifyingly perceptive understanding that saw past his discipline straight to the exhaustion he refused to acknowledge.
"Sit anyway," she said, her voice softening but retaining its iron core. "Let me do this..."
"I want to."

It was a pathetic, automatic gesture, the action of a man whose hands needed a purpose because his mind was drowning in something he refused to name.
Diana was still standing near Rex, her chest still rising and falling from the exertion, when she sensed his approach.
She turned, wiping sweat from her brow, and her expression shifted instantly.
The warmth she had shown Rex vanished, replaced by the polished, impenetrable neutrality of a trained operative.
"Thank you," she said, reaching for the towel.
Her voice was flat, stripped of inflection, carrying nothing but the hollow courtesy she would extend to a stranger.
Theo didn’t retreat.
"You have improved," he said, his voice carrying a strained edge that he couldn’t quite suppress.
"Since yesterday... the change is... not subtle."
"He is a good teacher," Diana replied.
She didn’t look at him.

She began wiping the salt from her neck, her body language already angling away from him in the precise, dismissive posture of someone who had already decided that this interaction was a tactical waste of time.
"I could see that," Theo said, his jaw tightening.
He stood there for a moment, the silence between them stretching uncomfortably long, filled only by the distant sounds of other fighters resuming their drills.
Then, driven by some desperate, ill-advised impulse, the kind that makes men ruin themselves, he pushed further.
"We used to spar together... before all of this and before the House became... this.
You remember."
Diana paused mid-motion.
For a heartbeat, something flickered behind her eyes, a ghost of a memory, but it was gone before it could take root.
"I remember," she said coldly.
"We were fifteen..."
"You broke my wrist because you didn’t know how to control your own momentum, and I forgave you because we were children who knew nothing of consequence."
The memory hung between them like a blade.
Theo flinched almost imperceptibly at the reminder of his own past weakness, his fingers curling tighter around the towel.
"I have thought about that sometimes," Theo said, his voice dropping to something raw and almost vulnerable, though it still tasted of bitter regret.
"I’ve thought about how different everything might have been."
"How different we might have been if we had kept training together instead of drifting into separate circles."
Diana finally turned to face him fully.
The mask of polite neutrality didn’t just slip; it shattered.
The patience she had been extending that fragile, customary courtesy withered and died in her eyes.
"Theo," she said.
Her voice wasn’t loud, but it possessed a terrifying, razor-edged clarity that seemed to suck the air out of the immediate space around them.

"I am going to say this once, and I am going to say it clearly, because I think you are trapped in some delusion that if you say enough small things in enough quiet moments, something will eventually land differently than the last one did."
"You think you’re planting seeds...
You’re not."
Theo opened his mouth to speak, but she cut through him like a blade through silk.
"It will not happen...
I am not drifting back toward you."
"There is no version of the last several months, no timeline, no alternative reality where that happens."
"I did not choose Rex because you were unavailable, or because the timing was wrong, or because I was looking for an escape."
"I chose him because I love him... plainly, violently, and with a certainty I have never felt for anyone else." Her gaze hardened, becoming something cold and unforgiving.
"And every time you find some pathetic excuse to stand near me and invoke memories from when we were fifteen, it doesn’t make me nostalgic, Theo."
"It doesn’t make me remember a lost connection...
It makes me uncomfortable and it makes me want to walk away from you."
Theo’s jaw tightened so hard the muscles along his temple visibly pulsed.
His hands clenched into fists at his sides, the knuckles whitening.
The humiliation was visible in the way his shoulders tensed, a predator caught in a trap of his own making.
"I was not trying to make you uncomfortable," he said, his voice strangled, defensive, and dangerously thin.
"I know you weren’t trying to," Diana said.
Her expression shifted then.
The anger ebbed away, leaving behind something far more devastating: pity.
It was a soft, hollow sound in her voice that cut deeper than any insult.
"That is actually the worst part of this, Theo."
’You aren’t doing this maliciously...
You don’t even realize you’re doing it."
"Which means you don’t know how to stop, which means this cycle will continue until you finally develop the spine to actually let me go..."
"I cannot make that decision for you, and I cannot grieve the ghost of our childhood for you."
She didn’t wait for his rebuttal.
She didn’t give him the satisfaction of watching him break.
She simply turned her back on him, a dismissal more absolute than any physical blow, and walked back toward the center of the training floor.
Her destination was Rex.
He was standing there, framed by the afternoon light filtering through the high windows, engaged in a low-voiced conversation with Aurelia about the afternoon’s tactical schedule.
He hadn’t moved, hadn’t flinched, and hadn’t broken eye contact with the matriarch, but Rex was not a man who missed details.
He had heard every syllable of the exchange, every inflection of Diana’s pain and Theo’s desperation, yet he remained as impassive as carved granite.
Theo remained frozen at the wall.
His fingers curled reflexively around the empty air where the towel had been, his hand grasping at nothing.
He stood there, a disgraced prince in his own kingdom, watching the woman he wanted walk toward the man who had already won.
The training session dragged on for another hour, stretching long past the point where most of the observers had drifted away to their respective obligations.
The hall gradually emptied, the echoing shouts and the rhythmic clatter of weapons fading until the space held only those with a genuine reason or obsession to remain.
Aurelia moved through the remaining crowd like a queen surveying her domain, dismissing the last of the junior guards with crisp, unyielding instructions for the afternoon’s duties.
Iris departed with a subtle alertness in her step, leaving to investigate something at the household’s outer perimeter that had been gnawing at her assassin instincts since sunrise.
Elaris left last, carrying the unmistakable, buoyant energy of someone who had gained far more entertainment from watching the morning’s drama than she had anticipated.
Rex remained.
He began a final, solitary drill, the kind of brutal, punishing conditioning work that Martial Arts Mastery did not strictly require for combat efficiency but that his body demanded for survival.
It was the raw discipline of maintaining the foundation upon which his lethal abilities rested.

His movements were mechanical yet explosive; he moved through shadow boxing sequences that looked more like controlled strikes against invisible throats, followed by explosive bursts of footwork that left scuff marks on the stone.
By the time he finally ceased, the hall felt cavernous and still.
His shirt was soaked through, clinging to the hard planes of his chest like a second skin, and his breathing came in deep, ragged draws.
This was not the performed exhaustion of a demonstration; it was the honest, bone-deep fatigue of a body that had been pushed to its absolute limit for three consecutive hours.
Diana was already there, waiting at the edge of the floor.
She didn’t greet him with words; she simply existed there, a steady presence in the quiet hall.
As he approached, she handed him a cup of water.
He took it without ceremony, drinking half of it in desperate, greedy gulps, feeling the cold liquid cut through the furnace of his throat.
When he finished, she took the empty cup and reached for a fresh towel.
"Sit," she commanded.
Her voice was quiet, but it carried the weight of an order he wouldn’t or couldn’t refuse.
"You have been standing since before dawn, Rex."
"I am fine," he said.
The words were true; his body was built for this, forged in fires far hotter than a morning drill, but he knew it wasn’t the point.
He could see it in the way her jaw set, the way her eyes traced the tension in his shoulders.
Diana’s expression didn’t waver.
She didn’t argue, because she didn’t need to.
She simply stared at him with that terrifyingly perceptive understanding that saw past his discipline straight to the exhaustion he refused to acknowledge.
"Sit anyway," she said, her voice softening but retaining its iron core.
"Let me do this..."
"I want to."

chapters.title: Chapter 912. He Was Always Too Late, Now He’s Also Too Sad About It
paragraphs: Rex sank onto the wooden bench along the hall’s side wall, the muscles in his legs protesting the sudden cessation of movement. Diana didn’t hesitate; she knelt between his knees, claiming the space beside him with the casual certainty of someone who belonged there.

She began working the towel over his shoulders and neck, her movements unhurried and deliberate. This wasn’t the efficient wiping of sweat from a soldier; it was the meticulous care of a woman tending to the man she loved.

Her hands moved with a gentleness that bypassed all tactical training, a tenderness born from the raw honesty of that first night when they had stopped pretending and admitted exactly what they wanted from each other.
"You worked harder than you needed to today," she murmured.

Her thumbs found the knots of tension that had calcified along his traps during those final, punishing drills. She pressed in, working the muscle loose with a precision that was both therapeutic and intimate.
"You didn’t have to run that final conditioning set... Nobody was watching by then. Even the guards had gone."
"I was watching," Rex said, his voice gravelly from exertion. "That was reason enough."

Diana’s hands faltered for a heartbeat, that infinitesimal pause that signaled she was absorbing the weight behind his words. She didn’t speak, but the way she resumed her work, pressing deeper into his shoulders with a renewed firmness, spoke volumes.
She moved down his spine, each pass of the towel a caress, each press of her palms a silent acknowledgment of the burden he carried.
"You’re getting good at this," Rex noted, closing his eyes as the relief began to spread through his overheated frame.

"I’ve had excellent motivation to practice," Diana replied, a trace of amusement softening her tone. "You come home looking like you’ve gone through a meat grinder more often than either of us would ever admit aloud."
Silence settled between them as she continued, her hands tracing the rugged lines of his shoulders before moving down to his forearms, wiping away the salt and grime.

In this moment, Rex allowed himself something he granted almost no one else: he allowed the performance to drop. The director, the strategist, the weapon—all of it receded, leaving only the man beneath.
He let himself simply exist in her presence, anchored by the steady rhythm of her breathing and the heat of her touch.
When she finally finished, she didn’t rise. She remained kneeling between his legs, looking up at him.

Her face was flushed, her eyes bright with a quiet, satisfied hunger that mirrored his own. She reached up, her palm splaying across his damp chest where his heart still hammered against his ribs, and pulled him down into a kiss.

It was a slow, unhurried, and devastatingly honest kiss that tasted of sweat and shared secrets. Rex met her halfway, his hands finding her waist, giving himself to her with the kind of vulnerability that only existed in the spaces where they were truly alone.
The moment was absolute. Until it wasn’t.
Near the far entrance of the hall, where the shadows pooled thickest, a figure froze.
Theo had returned. It was a genuine errand; he needed the training log Aurelia kept on the shelf by the door, a mundane administrative task that fell to him as the heir whether he desired it or not.
He had expected an empty hall, a place of echoing stone and fading echoes. He had not expected to walk into the raw, unguarded aftermath of something so private, something so achingly obvious.

From his position in the doorway, he saw them: the way Diana leaned into Rex, the way Rex’s fingers curled possessively against her skin, the way they seemed to form a single, impenetrable unit of heat and devotion.
The sight hit him harder than any physical blow, a visceral ache that settled in his chest like broken glass.
He should have turned around immediately. He should have retreated into the darkness and pretended he had seen nothing.
But he remained motionless, trapped in the doorway, a ghost watching the living claim a happiness he could never touch.

Theo remained frozen in the doorway, a silent voyeur to a reality he could no longer claim. He stood there for several heartbeats longer than any sane man would, long enough to see the way Diana’s fingers curled possessively against Rex’s damp skin, long enough to see the unguarded softness in her jaw that he had never once been able to provoke.

Watching them was like watching a language he had forgotten how to speak being spoken fluently by two strangers. There was an ease between them, a seamless synchronization of breath and touch that had never existed between him and Diana, not even during those feverish summers when they had been inseparable.

Even then, there had always been a barrier, an unspoken distance that neither had dared to bridge. Now, seeing that barrier obliterated by Rex, Theo felt something in his chest tighten with the excruciating ache of witnessing something you desired belong completely and irrevocably to someone else.
’It isn’t fair,’ a small, venomous part of his mind hissed.

It was the same furious, wounded voice that had spoken to him years ago on the rain-slicked streets when he had thrown a desperate punch he couldn’t back up, a punch he was still paying for in blood and reputation.

It wasn’t fair that Rex had simply walked into this house and claimed the territory Theo had spent half his life trying to map. Rex hadn’t fought for it; he had simply taken what Theo had spent years failing to build.

But as he watched Diana, really watched her, the fury began to curdle into something more painful: honesty. He saw the way her eyes closed when Rex kissed her, a surrender that wasn’t weakness but a profound choice.
He saw the genuine, unforced light in her expression. A quieter, more devastating part of him understood the truth that his pride refused to acknowledge: fairness had nothing to do with this.
Diana was not a trophy to be seized or a territory to be conquered. She had never been his to lose in the first place.
He had spent years operating under the quiet, arrogant assumption that she was simply waiting for him to become the man she needed, never realizing she had already found him in someone else.
The humiliation burned in his throat like bile, but he forced himself to move.

With movements practiced and precise, he stepped toward the shelf. His fingers brushed the leather binding of the training log, retrieving it without making so much as a whisper of sound against the wood.
He clutched it to his chest like a shield, a pathetic substitute for the connection he craved.
He turned and retreated into the shadows of the corridor, walking back the way he had come. He moved like a ghost, careful not to let his boots scrape or his breathing falter.
Behind him, in the warm glow of the training hall, Rex and Diana remained locked in their own private world, oblivious to his presence and pain.
Neither of them noticed him leave. Neither of them looked up. And as the darkness of the hallway swallowed him whole, Theo realized that their indifference was the most brutal answer of all.
The night did not bring relief; it only brought silence, and in the silence, the echoes were louder.

Theo lay flat on his back in the darkness of his chambers, the moonlight filtering through the high windows in cold, silver ribs across the ceiling. His room, designed with the austere elegance of a Nightwing heir, felt less like a sanctuary and more like a gilded cage.
He stared upward at the vaulted rooftop, his eyes tracing the familiar patterns of stone and shadow, but his mind was leagues away, trapped in the memory of the training hall.

Every time he closed his eyes, he saw them. He saw the way Diana had looked at Rex, not with the guarded respect she gave the guards or the polite distance she gave him, but with a raw, terrifying vulnerability.
That look had been a blade, twisting in the wound of his own inadequacy.
’I was too late,’ he thought, the realization settling in his gut like poisoned lead. ’I was always too late...’
He replayed the years like a broken film reel. He remembered the moments he had mistaken for connection, the times he had stood near her, offering nothing but the hollow expectations of his station.

He remembered how he had been so consumed by his own training, his own rise to power, and his own desperate need to prove he was worthy of the House that he had failed to see the girl standing right beside him.

He had been so insensitive, so utterly blind to the quiet ways she had reached for him, only to have him recoil into duty or retreat into arrogance. He had assumed she would always be there, a constant, a fixed point in his orbit, never imagining that even the most patient flame eventually burns out when left in the cold.
A memory surfaced, unbidden and cruel. They were fourteen.
