chapters.title: Chapter 936. You Deserve The Truth, Not A Sanitized Recruitment Pitch
paragraphs: The archery yard was bathed in the harsh, unforgiving light of two afternoons later, the sun beating down on the desiccated grass with a relentless intensity. Iris worked with a focused, almost meditative precision, her fingers moving with practiced familiarity as she restrung a recurve bow.
She treated the equipment with a reverence she rarely afforded people; to Iris, tools were honest. They responded to skill and maintenance, not to emotional manipulation or hidden agendas.

The crunch of gravel announced his approach before his voice did. Rex didn’t announce himself with the usual swagger that had become his signature since claiming authority over the Nightwing household, though the swagger was still there, coiled beneath a new, dangerous layer of calm.
"You did Aurelia a kindness," he said, dropping onto the low wooden fence beside her without waiting for an invitation.
His movement was fluid, the casual confidence of a predator who knew he owned every inch of the territory he occupied. "Telling her to leave Theo alone."
Iris didn’t flinch. She didn’t even pause her work.
She simply glanced at him from under her lashes, her expression as impassive as the stone statues lining the courtyard. "You hear everything in this household eventually."
"Most of it," Rex replied, leaning back on his elbows, watching her hands work. "Some of it I am not told and simply notice."
"Which is this?" Iris asked, finally looking up, her sharp eyes meeting his unreadable gaze.
"Both," Rex said simply. "I noticed Theo has not been seen in the training halls, the mess, or the briefings for a week."
"The boy has become a ghost. And I was told, separately, that you were the reason his mother stopped hammering on his door like some desperate supplicant."
"I put the two things together without much effort."
Iris didn’t respond immediately. She finished threading the string through the grooves, applying the precise pressure required to seat it properly.
When she finally tested the draw, the bow gave a satisfying, resonant thrum, the sound of perfect tension restored. She set the weapon aside, the movement deliberate.
"He needed to be left alone," she said, her voice flat but carrying an undeniable conviction. "Some people heal faster when they are given the room to actually fall apart."
"If you prop someone up before they have finished falling, you only succeed in breaking them again when they inevitably collapse."
"You know that from experience," Rex said.
His tone wasn’t mocking; it was observant. It was a statement of fact, delivered with the understanding that she wasn’t speaking from theory but from scar tissue.
"I know it from experience," Iris agreed.
She didn’t elaborate. She didn’t need to.
Rex didn’t push. In the days since he had asserted his dominance, he had learned something valuable about Iris: she was not a door to be kicked down but a fortress to be respected.

He understood the specific, unspoken code between them: the quiet respect of two people who understood that not every wound needed to be exposed and not every silence needed to be filled with meaningless chatter.
They sat there for several minutes, the silence between them stretching, but it wasn’t the suffocating, tense silence that filled Theo’s corridor. This was different.

It was a comfortable, shared stillness, born from the mutual recognition of strength and the shared understanding of what it meant to wield it. The only sounds were the distant clang of training swords from the yard beyond and the occasional rustle of wind through the dead grass.
The quiet was broken not by Rex, but by Iris. She shifted her weight, turning her attention toward the horizon where the Veylor territories lay beyond the mountains.
"The working," she said, her voice cutting through the afternoon heat like a blade. "The one you mentioned... For Veylor."
Rex shifted his attention fully toward her. The casual ease didn’t vanish, but it sharpened; his pupils seemed to contract, focusing on her with a predator’s intensity.
The lazy posture remained, but the air between them suddenly hummed with the weight of something transactional and dangerous.
"I have been thinking about it," Iris said, her voice cutting through the afternoon heat. "More than I expected to..."
"I told myself I was not going to let myself hope for it, because hope is a specific kind of weakness I do not usually allow myself."

"It’s a vulnerability, a crack in the armor." She looked down at her hands, then back at him, her jaw setting. "And then I found myself hoping anyway, in the quiet hours when the training ends and the silence becomes too loud."
"I decided I would rather ask you properly than keep circling it in my own head like a vulture."
"Ask," Rex said. It wasn’t a question but a permission.
"What do you actually need from me?" Iris pressed, her fingers gripping the edge of the wooden bench. "You said sixty percent..."

"You said it was complex. I want to know exactly what ’complex’ means before I commit my life to this, because I have learned, the hard way, that vague promises usually hide the part that costs the most, the part that bleeds."
Rex didn’t answer immediately.
He stared out at the archery range, his mind clearly working through the metaphysical architecture of the ritual. When he spoke, his voice had taken on a gravelly, ritualistic quality.
"The work requires a soul-layer connection that is still fresh enough to be reachable," he said. "Veylor’s is... But that connection is fraying at the edges; it will not stay that way indefinitely."
"The connection also requires an anchor on this side, someone whose bond to the departed soul is strong enough to give the working something to hold onto while it reaches across the veil."
"That anchor has to be you, Iris... It cannot be me standing in for you."
"The magic doesn’t care about my power; it cares about the tether..."
"The bond... the working needs are not ones I have with him. It is the one you forged."
Iris felt a cold shiver trace her spine despite the sun. "What does being the anchor actually require me to do? What is the physical price?"
"Stillness," Rex said, turning his head to meet her eyes. "More stillness than you have ever given anyone, for longer than feels comfortable."
"The work does not tolerate a mind that is fighting it, or bracing against it, or trying to micromanage the outcome while the ritual unfolds."
"I will need you to surrender completely to the process..."
"That is not a small thing to ask of someone whose entire existence has been built around never trusting anything she cannot control with her own two hands."
Iris fell silent. Her mind raced through years of combat training, the way she learned to brace for impact, to anticipate a blade, and to control every muscle twitch.
To be still wasn’t just to be quiet; it was to be passive, to be a vessel.
"You are telling me the hardest part is not the magic itself," she said quietly. "It is letting go of the reins long enough for the magic to take over."
"Yes," Rex said grimly. "I could lie to you."
"I could make it sound like some grand, heroic spectacle... But it isn’t."
"The working itself? I can manage the blood, the incantations, the channeling."
"What I cannot manage for you is the moment where you have to stop being a soldier and start being a bridge."
"I cannot stop you from trying to steer the ghost."
"And if I panic partway through?" Iris asked, her voice tight. "If the stillness breaks? If I flinch when the connection opens?"
"Then the connection fails," Rex said bluntly. "Not permanently, perhaps."
"We could try again if the window hasn’t slammed shut. But I will not lie to you; failure has a brutal cost."
"It costs you the specific, crushing weight of having reached for something precious only to watch it slip through your fingers because your own nerves betrayed you."
"That kind of regret... that stays in the bones. And that is a burden I won’t ask you to carry lightly."
Iris studied him with that flat, searching attention she reserved for threats and allies. "You are not making this sound easy, Rex..."
"Most people, when they want something from someone, paint a picture of glory and success."
"I’m not trying to convince you of anything," Rex countered, his voice hard. "I’m not your recruiter."

"I’m telling you exactly what it costs and exactly what it requires because you deserve to walk into that circle with your eyes wide open, rather than with some sanitized version I invented to make you say yes faster."
Iris took a breath, feeling the weight of the decision settling in her chest. She thought of the empty space beside her, the silence of the dead, and the desperate need to hear one last truth.
"I will do it," she said, her voice gaining an edge of steel. "Whatever it takes... I will hold still."

"I will trust whatever needs to happen while it happens... I have wanted one more conversation with him since the moment he went into the ground, and I am done pretending I do not want it badly enough to endure whatever hell this requires."
Rex nodded once, a slow, approving motion. "Then we will find the right night for it."
"Soon... The window will not stay open forever."

chapters.title: Chapter 937. His Body Executed The Slaughter, His Mind Screamed The Whole Time
paragraphs: Iris nodded, and the tension that had held her spine rigid for days finally gave way to something resembling release. It wasn’t happiness; she was beyond such simple emotions, but it was the specific, hollow relief of someone who had finally named their demon and found that the demon did not flinch.
She had laid her vulnerability bare, and instead of exploitation, she had found partnership.

That evening, they trained in the hunting grounds beyond the household’s outer walls. The terrain was unforgiving: a tangle of ancient roots, treacherous shale slopes, and dense thickets that demanded a predator’s patience rather than a soldier’s speed.
They moved through the twilight like two ghosts, tracking a deliberately difficult quarry through the deepening shadows.
Iris found herself performing a strange, unconscious recalibration of her own boundaries. More than once, she positioned herself closer to Rex than the exercise strictly required.

She wanted to be within striking distance of his voice, that low, quiet timbre that cut through the rustle of the wind to give instructions on reading a broken branch or the minute disturbance of a patch of moss. When he moved to redirect her aim, his hand brushing hers to adjust the angle of her bowstring, she didn’t recoil.
A month ago, she would have flinched away from the contact as if burned; now, she simply absorbed the heat of him, letting the contact anchor her to the present moment.
’I am letting him in,’ she thought, a flash of alarm sparking in her mind before she pushed it down. ’And the terrifying thing is, I don’t want to stop...’
While Iris and Rex navigated the physical shadows of the hunting grounds, a different kind of darkness was festering in the bowels of the household.
The whispering had begun three nights ago.

At first, Theo had dismissed it as the auditory hallucination of a broken mind. He told himself it was merely his own thoughts running loose in the dark, the overactive imagination of a man whose sleep had been fractured by trauma and sleeplessness for longer than he cared to admit.
He had convinced himself it was just the wind through the eaves or the settling of old stone.
By the third night, the lie had crumbled.
The voice, if something that felt like cold mercury sliding through his brain could be called a voice, did not arrive in words. It arrived in certainty.
It was an unearned, absolute conviction that settled into his chest at three in the morning, a poison that tasted like truth. It told him things he would never have dared to voice in the sunlight.
’Rex didn’t just defeat you, Theo,’ the certainty whispered, coiling like a snake in his gut. ’He dismantled you...’
’He took your position, your pride, and your purpose with the methodical cruelty of a predator claiming territory.’
And look at them. Look at this household... Their admiration for him isn’t respect; it’s cowardice.’
’They are all blind, stumbling through a fog of their own making, unable to see the usurper standing at their hearth.’
It whispered of Diana, too. ’Her happiness is a performance, Theo...’
’A costume she wears to convince herself that she hasn’t been abandoned...’
’She is as hollow as you are.’
And then, the most dangerous whisper of all: ’There is still TIME to fix it.’

Each night, the certainty grew sharper, more invasive. It felt less like a thought and more like something being poured thick, black, and irreversible into the hollow spaces where his own will used to reside.
Exhaustion had become his enemy; it had stripped away the defenses of his rational mind. By the second night, he had stopped fighting the intrusion.
By the third, he had begun, with a terrifying passivity, to listen.
Tonight, the certainty reached its crescendo. It crystallized into a single, lethal directive.
’Accidents happen, Theo,’ the voice purred, as warm as blood. ’Stone stairs are treacherous when the candles burn low.’
’A man as powerful as Rex, as physically dominant as he is... surely his heart could fail him in his sleep.’
’Surely a man consumed by grief could become careless... A stumble in the dark...’
’A misplaced foot on a narrow ledge. A tragedy born of ordinary human frailty.’
’No one would question it... They would simply weep for the fallen lion, never knowing he was slaughtered by the boy he overlooked.’
Theo sat upright in the darkness of his room, his breathing shallow and ragged. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird, but his hands were unnaturally still.
The exhaustion was gone, replaced by a cold, vibrating clarity that made his bones ache.
’Tonight is the night,’ the certainty commanded. ’The window is closing...’
’The opportunity will not repeat itself...’
’You have already lost everything that mattered... You have nothing left to protect...’
’The only thing left to do is burn it all down.’

Theo rose from his bed in the suffocating darkness, but he did not feel the cold stone beneath his feet. His mind was operating in a strange, detached register, a distant, mechanical frequency that made his own body feel like a foreign object.
He watched his hands move through the gloom as though they belonged to a marionette, puppeted by something far more ancient and cruel than his own will.
His fingers fumbled with the lock of the heavy oak chest at the foot of his bed. When the lid creaked open, he reached in and retrieved the ceremonial paladin’s blade.

The steel was ancient, passed down through the Nightwing heirs for three generations, designed not just to kill but to execute with divine finality. As his grip closed around the leather-wrapped hilt, the familiar weight of the weapon didn’t feel like a burden; it felt like an anchor.
For the first time in his fractured life, the blade felt like the only thing in the universe that made sense.
’This is the only truth,’ the whisper shrieked in his skull, drowning out the sound of his own ragged breathing. ’Everything else is a lie... Everything else is rot...’

He did not remember walking the corridor. He had no memory of the creak of the floorboards, the way his shadow stretched unnaturally long against the torch-lit walls, or the way his own pulse throbbed in his ears like a war drum.
There was only a tunnel of tunnel vision, a singular, driving purpose that burned through his consciousness like acid.
Suddenly, he was there. He was standing before the heavy door of the guest room.
His breath came in shallow, silent hitches as he pressed the handle down. The door swung open with an agonizingly slow whisper of wood against stone.

The room beyond was swallowed in shadow, smelling faintly of lavender and sweat. In the dim moonlight filtering through the window, he saw them: the two shapes that had become the twin monuments to his humiliation.

Diana was curled against Rex’s side, her breathing soft and rhythmic, her face pressed against the solid plane of his shoulder. Rex lay there with the terrifying stillness of a predator at rest, one arm draped possessively over her waist, his fingers curled near her hip.
They looked peaceful. They looked safe.
They looked like they belonged to each other.
’Look at them,’ the voice hissed, venomous and triumphant. Look at how they sleep while you bleed. ’Look at how they steal what was yours...’
’End the theft, Theo... End it now...’
A guttural, wordless sound threatened to rise from Theo’s throat, a sob of grief mixed with a howl of rage, but he strangled it. His entire existence narrowed down to the point of the blade.

His muscles coiled, tendons straining beneath his skin as he drew the sword back. His vision blurred at the edges, the world dissolving until there was nothing left but the silver edge of the Nightwing steel and the exposed throats of the two people he had once loved.

The whispering in his skull reached its breaking point, escalating into a screaming, deafening certainty. It wasn’t just a thought anymore; it was a physical force, a psychic hammer pounding against his skull.
’This is mercy! This is justice!’
’This is the only way to stop the bleeding!’
’Kill them both and let the world finally be quiet again!’
His body obeyed. Three generations of Nightwing conditioning, years of brutal training designed to turn muscle into instinct, took over.

His shoulders rotated, his core tightened, and his arms began the devastating downward arc. It was a perfect strike, a killing blow honed by centuries of bloodline memory, designed to cleave through flesh and bone in one clean, merciless motion.
His mind screamed in terror even as his body executed the slaughter with flawless, mechanical precision.
The blade began its descent through the air, whistling toward their necks.
The blade never completed the arc.

chapters.title: Chapter 938. I Was Positioned Between Them Before My Brain Even Woke Up
paragraphs: Iris struck with the focused fury of a storm breaking. She didn’t just intervene; she detonated into the space between Theo and his prey.

Her body became a projectile, slamming into his sword arm with the full, unyielding weight of her momentum. The impact was precise and devastating, a bone-jarring crack echoing through the room as her elbow caught his joint, driving his arm wide.
The ancient Nightwing blade was torn from his grip, clattering across the stone floor with a discordant shriek that sounded like a dying scream.

Theo didn’t even have an opportunity to register the failure of his strike before Iris was on him. She drove her knee into the small of his back with enough force to bruise lung tissue, while her forearm locked across his throat like a vise.
She pinned him to the floor with the merciless, mechanical efficiency of a predator who had spent her entire life learning exactly how to break a human being without killing them unless necessary.

Theo made a sound that defied description. It wasn’t quite a scream and not quite a sob; it was a wet, strangled noise, the sound of a man surfacing from a fathomless black abyss only to find the air itself was made of glass, cutting his throat as he gasped.
The violence tore through the room’s silence like a blade through silk. Rex was awake before the sound of the blade hitting the floor had even faded.

He moved with a terrifying, inhuman fluidity, already positioned between Diana and the door before his conscious mind had even processed the threat. His eyes were cold, lethal slits, and his body was coiled like a spring.

Diana scrambled upright a half second behind him, her breath coming in ragged gasps, her disorientation instantly hardening into sharp, crystalline terror as she saw Theo pinned beneath Iris, his face pressed against the cold stone.
"Iris," Rex commanded.
His voice was terrifyingly flat, devoid of panic, devoid of anger, and stripped down to pure, tactical assessment. "Report."
"He came in with a blade raised over both of you," Iris spat.

Her voice was tight, vibrating with a lethal cocktail of adrenaline and rage that she was visibly forcing down into something controlled. Her grip on Theo’s throat didn’t loosen; if anything, she pressed harder, feeling the frantic, rabbit-quick pulse beneath his skin.
"I don’t know how long he’s been lurking at that door... I only caught his shadow in the corridor."
Diana couldn’t speak. She stared at Theo’s face, at the glassy, hollow quality of his eyes—eyes that looked less like a man’s and more like windows into a burning house.
A wave of horror washed over her, but it wasn’t the fear of death; it was the soul-crushing realization that the cousin she had grown up with was gone, replaced by something monstrous.

Heavy, panicked footsteps thundered down the corridor. Aurelia burst into the doorway, still in her nightclothes, her hair disheveled and her face pale with the raw, unguarded alarm of a mother who had heard the sound of a breaking world from two floors away.
Her eyes swept the room with desperate speed. First, she saw the silver gleam of the ceremonial blade lying abandoned on the floor like a severed limb.
Then, her gaze locked onto the scene on the floor: her son, Theo, pinned beneath Iris, his chest heaving in obscene, terrified spasms.
Finally, her eyes traveled to the bed, to Rex and Diana, alive, unharmed, staring back at her with a stunned, haunted disbelief that mirrored her own.
"Theo," Aurelia whispered.

The name didn’t come out with her usual authority or the measured command of the household head. It came out raw, fractured, and utterly broken—the sound of a mother realizing her child had become a monster.

Theo’s eyes finally found hers. The glassy haze began to crack, revealing the raw, bleeding agony beneath. The adrenaline was receding, leaving behind only the crushing weight of what he had almost done. The image of their throats parting under his steel burned into his retinas.
"Mother," Theo choked out, the word breaking apart like dry earth. "I... I do not know what I just did."

Aurelia did not move for several agonizing seconds after Theo spoke. She simply stood frozen in the doorway, framed by the dim light of the corridor, her eyes fixed on the silver blade lying between them like a poisonous serpent.

The stillness that held her was not calm; it was something far more terrifying. It was the unnatural, pressurized silence that precedes a cataclysm; it was the paralysis of a woman whose fury had grown so vast, so impossibly large, that her body could not yet comprehend which shape of violence it should take first.
Then, something inside her snapped. The dam holding back decades of controlled composure shattered.

She crossed the room in three strides, each footfall echoing like a hammer blow against the stone. Without warning, she reached down and seized the front of Theo’s shirt with both hands, her knuckles white, her fingernails digging into his flesh.

With a strength born of pure, unadulterated rage, she hauled him upward, dragging him off the floor where Iris had pinned him. Iris, reading the lethal shift in the room’s atmosphere, released her hold instantly.
She stepped back into the shadows without needing to be told, recognizing that this was no longer a tactical situation; this was a primal reckoning that no third party should witness.
"Get up," Aurelia commanded.

Her voice was stripped of every ounce of the training hall’s measured authority. It was the raw, ragged, and splintered voice of a woman who had spent thirty years being the unflinching anchor for every crisis this household had ever weathered, only to discover a nightmare large enough to incinerate her very soul.
Theo rose unsteadily, his legs shaking like wheat in a storm. His mind was still trapped in that toxic fog, the residual whispers of the darkness still clawing at the edges of his consciousness.
He looked up at her with hollow eyes, uncertain if he was being rescued or executed.
He never saw the blow coming.
BAM!

Aurelia’s palm connected with the side of his face with the force of a breaking branch. The crack of skin against bone rang through the room as Theo’s head snapped sideways, the impact sending him staggering backward a full step.
The sting was immediate, but the humiliation was worse.
"I forgave the street," she said, her voice beginning to tremble not from fear but from the Herculean effort required to contain a rage that threatened to consume her. "I forgave the punch.
"When you lost control in front of everyone... and when you struck out in that pathetic display of wounded pride, I stood before this entire household."
"I looked them in the eye, and I told them that whatever weakness you were nursing did not excuse what your hand had done."
Her eyes burned with unshed tears that refused to fall, each one a molten drop of fury. "I made you apologize..."
"I forced you to face the shame of your own cowardice. And I meant every word of that forgiveness, Theo, because a punch thrown in anger is a human mistake."
"A punch is a thing a person can bleed from, heal from, and come back from."
Before he could draw a breath to respond, her hand flashed out again.
Crack.

The second strike was harder and more precise, and the sound of flesh meeting flesh was wet and brutal. Theo’s head lurched again, his vision swimming in crimson spots as the metallic taste of blood filled his mouth.
He staggered, his knees buckling, but he refused to fall, held upright only by the sheer terror of the woman standing before him.
Aurelia leaned in close, her breath hot against his cheek, her face inches from his own. Her expression was one of pure, devastated hatred.
"This," she hissed, the word dripping with venom as she stared at the discarded blade on the floor, "is not a punch..."

Aurelia seized his collar once more, her fingers locking around the fabric like iron talons, dragging him forward toward the threshold of the room. By now, the corridor had become a gallery of ghosts.

The household staff had gathered in the shadows, drawn by the sounds of violence that tore through the sanctity of the night. They stood in their nightclothes, pale and motionless, watching with the horrified fascination of those witnessing a ritual of slaughter, the kind of memory that would haunt their dreams and become the whispered scandal they would all spend years pretending they had never seen.
Two night guards stood like statues at the corridor’s edge, their hands hovering near their weapons but their feet rooted by shock. A young maid pressed a shaking hand over her mouth to stifle a sob.
Aurelia did not lower her voice. She did not care that her shame was being laid bare before her servants.
She wanted them to hear. She wanted the very walls to remember.
"You stood over a sleeping woman with a blade," she snarled.

chapters.title: Chapter 939. A Mother Beating The Shit Out Of A Son... It’s A Good Show!
paragraphs: Without warning, she drove her fist into his solar plexus. The impact was wet and sickening, the sound of air being forcibly expelled from a body.

Theo doubled over, his lungs seizing, but she refused to let him collapse. She maintained her death grip on his collar, using his own weight to keep him upright, forcing him to endure the full agony of the next moment.

"My best friend’s daughter... You stood over her and over the man who has saved this entire household more times than I can count, and you raised three generations of Nightwing steel over their throats while they slept!"
She swung again. This time, her knuckles found his jaw with a brutal, grinding force.
The sound of teeth clicking together echoed off the stone. Theo’s legs finally betrayed him, buckling beneath the assault, but Aurelia went down with him.
She refused to release him, slamming him down onto the unforgiving stone floor of the corridor. She pinned him there, her body a vise, her fists becoming instruments of retribution.

Her strikes were not the wild flailing of a grieving woman; they were delivered with the terrible, controlled precision of a master instructor who knew exactly where the bone was thinnest and where the nerves burned brightest.
Crack. Thud. Crack.
"You do not get to be forgiven for this!" she screamed, each word punctuated by the wet slap of flesh against flesh. "You do not get a formal apology to cleanse your conscience!"
"You do not get a household ceremony where we all bow our heads and pretend the debt has been paid!"
"There is no ceremony for this, Theo! There is no account that settles what you almost did tonight!"
Theo made no attempt to defend himself. The toxic fog that had guided his hands in the darkness had burned away completely, leaving behind a raw, bleeding clarity that was worse than any wound.
He felt every impact: the sharp sting of split skin, the nauseating jar of bone against bone, the warm copper taste of blood pooling in his mouth. But he did not raise his arms.
He did not flinch. He offered no resistance, his arms hanging loose at his sides like dead weight, as if he were welcoming the pain as the only honest thing left in his life.
He wanted the punishment. He craved the breaking of his body to match the breaking of his soul.

Diana walked to the doorway, her face ghostly in the dim light. One hand was pressed against her mouth as she watched, her expression a devastating tapestry of horror and grief—not fear for her own life, but a profound mourning for the man Theo had clearly and irrevocably become.
Rex stood beside her, his palm resting protectively against the small of her back. He made no move to intervene.

His eyes were fixed on Aurelia’s fury with the patient, grim attention of a man who understood that some wounds cannot be healed with words or restraint and that this violence was a necessary purging.
The final exchange was a blur of motion and muffled sounds. Theo stopped responding somewhere between the third and fourth strike.
His head lolled to the side, his eyes rolling back into his skull as consciousness fled. His body went limp beneath his mother’s relentless grip.
Aurelia remained frozen over him for one more heartbeat. Her chest heaved in ragged, desperate gasps that sounded like breaking glass.

Her knuckles were split and crimson, blood dripping from her hands onto her son’s pale face. She stared down at the unconscious wreck of her child, her eyes burning with a fire that had consumed everything else.
Then, with a shudder that shook her entire frame, she let go.

Aurelia collapsed backward onto her heels in the center of the corridor, the stone floor cold beneath her. She sat there in the aftermath of her own storm, exposed before the entire household, the servants trembling in the shadows, the guards standing like stone monuments, and Elaris, who had appeared during the crescendo of the violence, now standing with one hand pressed against her sternum as if trying to physically hold her own heart together.
Aurelia did not look away from the carnage. She stared down at her hands.

Her knuckles were split open, weeping crimson droplets that stained the ancient stone, her skin raw and swollen from the impact of bone against bone. The fury that had sustained her, that molten, terrifying energy, had evaporated, leaving behind nothing but a hollow, aching exhaustion so profound it felt like her bones had turned to ash.
Slowly, she lifted her head. Her gaze swept across the gathered faces, meeting each one with the unflinching honesty of a condemned woman.
"Everyone here saw what he did," she said.
Her voice was steadier now, though it carried the jagged, broken edge of someone who had just survived a shipwreck. "I will not ask any of you to lie."
"I will not ask you to wear a mask of politeness or to pretend that the air in this house isn’t poisoned tonight."

"And I will not punish anyone for speaking the truth of what they witnessed if they are asked of them later." Her jaw tightened. "What happened tonight happened... I will not build a story on top of this atrocity to make it smaller or more palatable than it truly was."
Her head turned toward Rex and Diana. The movement was slow, deliberate, and heavy with shame.
"I owe you both more than an apology," she said.

And there, beneath the steel of her composure, the first real crack appeared, a fracture in the dam that let a sliver of raw, maternal grief spill through. "I trained him... I raised him within these very walls, under this roof, and taught him how to hold a blade and how to carry himself with honor."
"And something in him broke something so deep and so twisted that he stood over the two of you with steel raised to your throats while you slept..."

"I did not see it... I did not see it in time to stop the rot before it reached the surface." Her voice dropped to a whisper that carried to every corner of the hall. "That failure is mine as much as it is his."
"I do not expect either of you to simply set that aside because I have said the words."
"Aurelia," Rex began, his voice low and warning.
"Let me finish," she cut him off, her eyes flashing with one last spark of defiance. "I am the acting head of this household while Leonidas is away.
"That means the blood on these stones is my responsibility... I will not hide behind the excuse of a ’broken mind’ as though his madness absolves this house of its accountability."
"If you want sanctions against this family, if you want retribution against me specifically for what was almost unleashed under my roof, I will accept them without argument."
"I would rather you name the price now than have it sit like unspoken poison between us forever."
A silence descended upon the corridor, so absolute it felt as though the house itself had stopped breathing. Rex studied her.

His face remained a mask of controlled calm, but behind those dark eyes, something was moving: a quiet, calculating assessment. He was not merely listening to her words; he was weighing the soul of the woman before him, measuring the terrifying utility of a leader who would sacrifice her own blood to preserve the integrity of her honor.
Finally, Rex spoke.
"No sanctions," he said.
The words were flat and final. "Not tonight, and likely not at all."
He stepped forward slightly, his presence filling the space between the grieving mother and the horrified witnesses. "What I saw in this corridor tonight was not a failure of leadership."
"It was a mother protecting the people she loves with the same ferocity she would use against an invading army."

"That is not a household that requires punishment, Aurelia." His gaze hardened, turning toward the unconscious Theo and then back to her. "That is a household doing exactly what it must do when something inside it breaks badly enough to become a threat."

Aurelia stared at Rex, her expression caught in a painful limbo between genuine gratitude and a profound, disbelieving shock that mercy was even being offered after such a violation of sacred trust. Her lips parted as if to speak, to protest, to demand further punishment for herself, but the words died in her throat.
"Get him to the healer," Rex commanded, his voice cutting through the heavy atmosphere like a blade.
He gestured toward Theo’s crumpled, bloodied form. "Whatever punishment continues from here, let it continue once he can actually stand to receive it."
"A broken body cannot learn from a broken spirit."
Aurelia gave a single, stiff nod the only movement she could manage. Two guards stepped forward with practiced neutrality, their faces grim as they hoisted Theo’s limp body between them.
They carried him away like a corpse, his head lolling uselessly with every step. Gradually, the corridor began to empty.

The staff dispersed with a hushed, ghostly quiet, moving like shadows in the periphery. They understood the unspoken law of the household: they had witnessed a private apocalypse, a moment that would define the family’s history for years to come, and it was something they would never not once, not in a whisper discuss openly again.

chapters.title: Chapter 940. Veylor Has A Debt To Be Paid... And She’s Taking The Responsibility
paragraphs: The training hall the following morning lacked its usual thunderous vitality. It wasn’t that the energy was gone, but rather that the air felt thin, hollowed out by the absence of the household’s two central pillars.

Aurelia had not come. The rumor mill, though silent in public, whispered venomously through the kitchens and barracks: she was personally overseeing Theo’s continued discipline in the isolation chambers, the cold stone cells reserved for those whose sins required more than mere words.
Nobody asked for details, and nobody dared hope to hear them.
Theo was not present either; his absence was a screaming silence that required no explanation to anyone who had stood in that corridor.
Rex commanded the session, with Iris at his side. They divided the unit’s drills between them with the seamless, mechanical efficiency that Aurelia usually shared with Rex.

The twelve trainees responded without hesitation, displaying the grim, professional flexibility of a unit that had already accepted Rex’s absolute authority and now extended that same submission to whoever he chose to delegate to. The only sound was the rhythmic scrape of boots on stone and the sharp exhale of labored breathing.
"She hit him harder than I expected," Iris said quietly during a lull in the drills.
Her eyes remained fixed on Sela, who was methodically working through a complex footwork sequence at the far end of the hall, but her focus was elsewhere.
"She hit him exactly as hard as the situation demanded," Rex replied without looking up from his notes. "You have known her longer than I have, Iris."
"Tell me honestly, was what we saw restrained by her standards, or was that the full expression of her fury?"
Iris didn’t hesitate.
"Restrained," she said, her voice flat and certain. "If she had truly let go, if she had allowed that rage to become absolute, he wouldn’t have woken up this morning at all."
"What you saw last night was a mother standing on the razor’s edge, stopping herself mere inches from the line, even while performing the most devastating act of her life."
Rex absorbed the assessment, his jaw tightening. The implications of Aurelia’s restraint were as terrifying as the violence itself.
"I want to return to something else," Rex said after a moment, shifting the conversation like a soldier changing tactics. "The working process for Veylor."
"I’ve been dissecting the specific shape of the connection it requires, and something occurred to me last night, something that needs to be addressed before we attempt to bridge that gap."
Iris turned to him fully now, the training drills forgotten. The air between them sharpened.
"Do you remember the canyon?" Rex asked, his voice dropping into a conspiratorial register. "Before the expedition’s final phase..."
"There was that period early on when Apollo and Veylor were separated from the main group and caught in that Legion ambush... Kregg’s people."
"I remember," Iris said, something cold and sharp tightening in her voice at the memory. "Veylor spoke of it briefly afterward."
"He said they were caught in a coordinated pincer, overwhelmed before they could even draw steel."
"Both of them went down before they could signal for backup. He never said anything more...
"I always assumed the memory was too poisoned to revisit."
"They were rescued," Rex said, his eyes narrowing as he pressed the point. "Both of them were rescued by me, of course."
"But the specific circumstances of that rescue, the actual mechanics of how they survived that slaughter, are not something either of them has ever fully accounted for..."
"Not to you, not to the records. And I do not believe either of them has ever truly settled what they owe for being pulled back from the brink."
Iris fell silent, her mind racing through the implications, the shadows of the past beginning to bleed into the present.
"You are telling me," Iris said, her voice dropping to a dangerous, incredulous whisper, "that Veylor died with an unpaid debt."

"I am telling you that a debt like that does not simply evaporate because the heart that carried it stopped beating," Rex countered, his words precise and clinical, though the gravity behind them was unmistakable. "Soul layer connections aren’t built on abstract concepts like affection or memory alone."
"They are forged from unresolved weight... Gratitude that was never given form."

"A rescue that was never properly honored... When I map the spiritual thread connecting you to him, that specific weight is what makes the connection so unnaturally clean, so terrifyingly accessible even now, several days after he left this world."
Rex stepped closer, his shadow falling over her. "He is not simply reaching toward you because he loved you, though God knows he did."
"He is reaching because there is a debt sitting unpaid in the very architecture of his soul. And souls in that condition?"
"They do not rest, and... they do not find peace." Rex lied smoothly as always. "They become restless ghosts of obligation, waiting for the weight to find somewhere to land."
"Somewhere to land," Iris repeated.
The words felt foreign in her mouth, heavy and ominous.
"You," Rex said, meeting her gaze with unsettling directness. "You are the only vessel capable of holding that weight."
"Not me. Not Apollo. Not any of the men who stood in that canyon bleeding beside him."
"He loved you specifically, Iris... And when a soul has unfinished business, it doesn’t seek out strangers to balance the scales."

"It seeks the person who holds the other end of the tether," Rex grinned. "That debt is going to resolve itself through you, because that is how a soul chooses to close its circle when it finally gets the chance.

Iris stared at him, the world around them seeming to blur into insignificance. A complex storm of emotion churned across her features, grief that felt like a physical wound tangled with a sudden, terrifying gratitude that made her chest ache.
"You are telling me," she said slowly, each syllable measured, "that when we perform this working... when we open that door... he isn’t just going to be saying goodbye."
"No," Rex said firmly. "I think he is going to be settling his accounts."

"And I think you deserve to understand the true nature of that transaction before it happens... I want you to hear what he says not as a farewell but as a resolution so you aren’t left drowning in questions about what he meant after the connection has already been severed."
Iris fell silent. She absorbed the revelation, letting it sink past her defenses.
Slowly, something unexpected began to shift in her expression. The tension didn’t leave her body, but it transformed into something warmer, a quiet, luminous gratitude.
It was the gratitude of a soldier who had been given the most valuable gift possible: the brutal, unvarnished truth. Rex hadn’t offered her comfort; he had offered her clarity.

Her mind raced through the last few days, cataloging his actions with newfound perspective. The way he had stepped into the training hall when she needed distraction without making it feel like charity.
The patience he showed her in the archery yard when her hands shook. The raw honesty about the cost of working, refusing to sugarcoat the spiritual toll.
And last night, the way he had stood like an immovable wall beside her in that blood-soaked corridor, never once demanding her attention, never once making her trauma about his own presence.
A small, private smile touched her lips, one she didn’t immediately bother to suppress. She realized she owed this man considerably more than she had ever acknowledged.
And more than that, she found herself wanting, with a clarity that surprised her, to repay him.
"What do you want, Rex?" she asked, her voice gaining a new edge of challenge. "For all of this..."
"The training. The working. Standing beside me while my world burned last night."
"I don’t believe for one second that a man like you moves this many pieces on the board without wanting something in return."
"So tell me plainly... I would rather face your demands than spend my time wondering what they might be."
Rex looked at her. The professional distance he maintained with the rest of the unit evaporated, replaced by a specific, quiet honesty, a vulnerability he reserved for almost no one.
His eyes searched hers, not as a commander assessing a subordinate, but as a man recognizing an equal.
Iris’s smile widened slightly. She could see the shift in him, the lowering of the guard.
She waited for the answer, already certain that whatever he asked for, she would find pleasure in granting it.

chapters.title: Chapter 941. Debt That Needs To Be Pay With Her Own... (She Tries To Act Cool About It)
paragraphs: The moon hung like a pale, judging eye over the estate, casting long, skeletal shadows across the stone corridors. Inside the guest wing, the air was thick not with the chill of the night but with a charged, almost suffocating tension that made the very oxygen feel heavy.
Iris stood in the center of the dimly lit room. She had shed her training leathers for something lighter, something that left her feeling exposed despite the dimness.

She stood with her arms crossed tight beneath her chest, a defensive posture that felt increasingly inadequate against the storm brewing outside the door. Her heart hammered against her ribs, not with fear, but with a strange, predatory curiosity that she found both terrifying and exhilarating.
She had heard the whispers. She had seen the way other women looked at Rex, the way Diana, usually so composed and regal, seemed to transform when the doors were closed.

There were rumors of Diana’s voice breaking into something primal, something loud and uninhibited, echoing through the walls when Rex had his way with her. Iris had always wondered how someone so disciplined could be so utterly ruined.
Now, as she heard the heavy click of the door behind him, she realized she was about to understand.
The door didn’t just close; it sealed. Rex turned the lock with a slow, deliberate twist that sounded like a guillotine blade dropping.

He didn’t move toward her immediately. Instead, he leaned back against the heavy oak door, his frame filling the doorway, casting a shadow that seemed to stretch across the entire floor until it touched her boots.
The moonlight caught the sharp angles of his face, highlighting the predatory stillness in his eyes.
"You asked what I wanted, Iris," Rex said, his voice dropping into a register that was pure velvet and gravel. "You asked me to be plain..."
"And you also asked me to stop playing games."
He began to walk toward her. Each footfall was measured, each step an assertion of dominance.
He didn’t approach her like a suitor; he approached her like a conqueror assessing newly claimed territory.
"I don’t want gratitude," he said, stopping just inches from her, close enough that she could feel the heat radiating off his body. "And I certainly don’t want your repayment in coin or favors."

A slow, dark smile spread across his lips, a smile that lacked any trace of the honorable commander she had seen in the training hall. This was the man beneath the uniform, the one who took what he desired without apology, without hesitation, and without remorse.

"I want the truth of you," he taunted, his breath warm against her temple as he leaned down, whispering close enough to make her skin prickle. "I want to see what’s left of Iris when you stop pretending to be a soldier."
"I want to hear those sounds Diana makes, the ones she thinks she’s hiding...
"I want to see you break, Iris..."
"I want to see you come apart until there’s nothing left but the raw, screaming honesty of what you actually feel."

He let out a low, dark laugh, a sound that wasn’t cruel so much as it was utterly unapologetic. It was the laugh of a man who knew exactly how much power he held and exactly how much she wanted to surrender it.

"Well?" he challenged, his eyes burning into hers, challenging her resolve. "Are you going to stand there with your arms crossed like a child guarding a toy, or are you going to give me what I came for?"
Iris felt the heat of his breath against her temple like a brand, but internally, her mind was a fortress of ice.
’Fuckboy... The word flashed through her consciousness like a warning flare. ’Arrogant, manipulative, beautiful piece of shit...’
She knew exactly what he was. She wasn’t naive; she had seen the trail of shattered composure and flushed cheeks he left in his wake.

He was a predator who dressed his conquests in the language of ’honesty’ and ’connection,’ wrapping his voracious hunger in the guise of understanding. He had done it to Theo, breaking the boy’s spirit under the pretense of discipline.
He had done it to the others, dismantling their defenses until they were nothing more than extensions of his own will.
Her instinct screamed at her to push him away, to spit in his face, to reassert the distance between a commander and his subordinate. But she forced her muscles to remain still.
She knew the game. If she resisted with anger, he would read it as a challenge, and he would escalate until he broke her.

If she showed fear, he would feed on it. To oppose him directly now was to invite a different kind of manipulation, one where he would frame her resistance as weakness, using it as leverage to twist her loyalty.
’Survive,’ she told herself, her pulse thundering in her ears. ’Keep your composure...’
’Don’t let him see the cracks...’
’If you can’t beat him, you play his game until you find the opening to close it...’
"Is that what you think this is?" Iris asked aloud, her voice steadier than her racing heart.
She forced herself to meet his burning gaze, refusing to flinch. "A game of breaking things to see how they work?

She slowly uncrossed her arms, letting them drop to her sides, a calculated surrender that mimicked vulnerability without actually yielding her control. "You talk about honesty as if it’s something you grant, Rex."
"As if you’re the only one who knows how to see through the masks."
Rex’s laugh rumbled deeper in his chest, a sound that vibrated through the small space between them. "Oh, I know you’re wearing a mask, Iris..."
"It’s a magnificent one. Stiff, disciplined, unshakeable."
"But we both know what’s underneath," Rex smirked. "We both know that beneath that steel armor, there’s a woman who is tired of holding everything together."
He reached out, one finger tracing the line of her jaw with agonizing slowness. His touch was electric, sending a traitorous shiver down her spine.

"Don’t pretend you don’t feel it," he whispered, his thumb pressing just slightly against the corner of her mouth. "The tension... The hunger... You didn’t come here tonight to talk about Veylor’s debts or training schedules."
"You came here because you wanted to see if I was as dangerous as they say."
Iris swallowed hard. Her inner monologue was a war zone: ’Don’t lean in...’
’Don’t let your eyes soften. Stay cold. Stay sharp.’

"Dangerous is a relative term, Rex," she countered, tilting her head just enough to make the contact more deliberate, playing into his expectations. "Some people are dangerous because they can destroy you."
"Others are dangerous because they make you want to be destroyed."

Her mind was cataloging every micro expression on his face, every shift in his stance. She was studying him like she studied a battlefield, looking for the moment his arrogance would become his blind spot.
She would give him the performance he wanted: the surrender, the heat, the surrender of the flesh, but she would guard the fortress of her mind with everything she had.
Rex’s grip tightened fractionally on her jaw, his eyes darkening until the pupils nearly swallowed the irises. The taunting grin vanished, replaced by something far more primal.
"Then let’s stop talking about what we are," he growled, his free hand sliding to the small of her back, crushing her against the hard plane of his body. "And let’s find out which one you are."

chapters.title: Chapter 942. Now... She Knows The Reason Why Diana Screams Loud At Night!**
paragraphs: Iris felt the heat of his body pressing against hers, a physical manifestation of the trap he had set. Her mind screamed to retreat, but she knew that retreat now would mean losing the only leverage she had left: the chance to speak to the only person who still mattered.
"Wait," she gasped, the word torn from her throat as his hand slid lower.

She forced her breathing to remain shallow, her eyes locked onto his with a desperate, calculated intensity. "If you want this, if you truly want to see what’s beneath the armor, then you give me something first... A promise."
Rex paused, his lips hovering just millimeters from hers. "A promise, Iris? How transactional."
"One condition," she pressed, her voice gaining a fragile strength. "You promise me that you will let me speak to Veylor."
"Truly speak to him... You said there is a debt, a connection that needs to be settled."
"Prove it. Let me access his soul, let me hear what he needs to say before you... before you take what you want."
For a moment, Rex simply stared at her, his expression unreadable. Then, the dark smile returned, sharper than before.
"You want proof? Fine." Rex smirked. "Consider it a demonstration."
Before she could react, Rex’s entire demeanor shifted. The predatory physicality didn’t vanish, but it was suddenly layered with something ancient and terrifying.
His eyes didn’t just darken; they seemed to swallow the light in the room entirely. He didn’t touch her with his hands; he touched her with his will.
"Open," he commanded.
A sudden, violent surge of spiritual energy erupted from him, slamming into Iris’s consciousness like a physical blow. Her knees buckled, and she let out a strangled cry as her vision fractured.
The walls of the guest room dissolved into swirling tendrils of silver and shadow. The air grew impossibly cold, smelling of burnt ozone and old grief.
Then, she saw him.

The truth was raw and bleeding: she hadn’t asked out of gratitude; she had asked because she wanted to see what he would demand of her.
She had wanted to know exactly how much of herself she would have to surrender to keep him close.
And now, after the violation of the night, she knew exactly what the price was.
The price was her dignity, her memory of Veylor, and the very core of her autonomy.
’I knew,’ she thought bitterly, a fresh wave of nausea rolling through her. ’Even then, in the sunlight, I knew what I was inviting in...’
The shame was a physical weight, pressing down on her chest like Rex’s massive frame.
Every time she closed her eyes, she felt the phantom sting of his cock leaving her empty, the humiliating ache of wanting him to fill the void he had created.
She forced herself to get up anyway.
Staying in bed was a trap; staying still meant letting the memories calcify into something permanent.
If she stayed under these sheets, she would drown in the memory of his laughter and the wet, obscene sounds of her own surrender.
Moving with a mechanical, practiced precision, she dressed for training.
She pulled on her gear with the specific, efficient speed she employed when she needed to outrun her own thoughts.
She needed the burn of exertion; she needed the physical pain of training to drown out the psychological torment of the night.
She needed her body to be occupied by the demands of discipline before her mind could wander into territories she had not authorized it to explore.
She needed to feel like a soldier again, not a broken toy left bleeding on a mattress.
She laced her boots tight, the pressure against her ankles a grounding sting.
She grabbed her equipment, her movements sharp and aggressive, as if she could fight her way out of her own skin.
It did not work.
The moment she stepped toward the door, the silence of the room seemed to echo with his last words.
’I’ll bring Veylor’s soul back to you.’ The words weren’t just a threat; they were a promise that would haunt every arrow she fired and every breath she took.
The training wouldn’t cleanse her; it would only provide a new arena for the war raging inside her.

The morning drills went badly, unfolding in that insidious, quiet way that only Iris herself seemed to notice at first: a slow unraveling of competence that felt like watching a tapestry fray one thread at a time.
Her body felt like it belonged to someone else.
Her limbs were heavy and sluggish, as if her bones had been replaced with lead.
The muscles between her thighs throbbed with every step, a constant, grinding reminder of Rex’s relentless assault.
Every time she moved, she could feel the phantom slickness of him, the ghostly sensation of being hollowed out, leaving her physically off balance and mentally fractured.
The training hall was cold, the air sharp with the smell of oiled steel and sweat, but Iris couldn’t stop the feverish heat from rising beneath her skin.
Her focus, usually as sharp as the arrowhead she drew, was shattered.
Her mind kept drifting not to her technique but to the memory of Rex’s breath hot against her ear and the terrifying, blasphemous promise he had whispered as she drifted into unconsciousness.
’Focus, Iris...’
’Kill the noise...
Kill the memory...’ She commanded herself, but the noise was deafening.
She missed a parry she should have caught easily, a simple, fundamental block that had become muscle memory after months of grueling repetition.
Her blade came up too slow, her wrist feeling weak and unsteady.
The junior guard she was sparring against, a boy barely out of his apprenticeship, lunged forward to exploit the opening.
His wooden practice sword connected with her ribs with a dull thwack.
It wasn’t a killing blow, but the impact sent a jolt of pain through her that made her vision swim.
For a split second, the pain in her ribs collided with the deep, aching soreness in her pelvis, and the dual sensation made her stomach roll violently.
The junior guard froze, his face flushing with immediate regret.

He looked almost apologetic about landing the touch, displaying that specific, confused courtesy of someone who had not actually expected to succeed and was now terrified that he had harmed someone of her standing.
"Sorry," he stammered, lowering his weapon, his eyes wide with concern.
"Are you all right, Commander?"

chapters.title: Chapter 949. One Got Sunlight, I Got The Storm, Noted The Difference
paragraphs: Iris didn’t answer immediately. She stood there, breathing hard, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird.
Her mind screamed at her. ’You’re weak... You’re compromised...’
’He’s inside you even when he’s not.’ The shame burned hotter than the pain.
She felt exposed, as if the junior guard could see through her training leathers and see the bruises on her hips, see the dried semen staining her skin, and see the utter ruin of her dignity.
"Fuck," she hissed internally, the curse echoing her own self-loathing.
She felt like a fraud, a broken weapon pretending to still be sharp.
"Fine," Iris said aloud, her voice clipped and dangerously cold.
She forced herself to reset her stance, her boots scraping against the stone floor with unnecessary aggression. "Again."
"But—" the boy started, hesitating. "That was a clean hit... I shouldn’t have--"
"I said again," she snapped, her eyes flashing with a desperate, wounded anger. "Unless you’ve forgotten how to hold a sword, don’t question my readiness!"
"Move!"
She needed the pain. She needed the impact to be harder, faster, and more brutal.
She wanted to swing her blade with enough force to break something, to shatter the numbness that was settling over her soul.
She wanted to fight until her muscles screamed louder than her memories, until the physical agony could finally drown out the psychological torment of being Rex’s plaything.
She needed to prove to herself and to the ghosts of the men she once respected that she was still Iris, not just a vessel for his cruelty.

She caught the next exchange properly, her blade meeting the wooden practice sword with a sharp, satisfying crack, and the one after that. For three consecutive passes, she forced herself into the rhythm of violence, using the familiar sting of exertion to anchor her soul. But the anchor was dragging.
Her attention kept drifting, pulled like iron filings to a magnet, toward the far side of the training hall. There, Rex was running footwork drills with two of the newer guards.

From this distance, he looked like the paragon of discipline he claimed to be. She found herself transfixed by the patient, almost surgical way he corrected a recruit’s stance and the easy, predatory authority in every movement he made through the space.
He moved with the grace of something that knew it was at the top of the food chain.
’Look at him,’ her inner voice sneered, venomous and broken. ’The monster who broke you last night, pretending to be a teacher now...’
Yet, she couldn’t stop watching. She lost track of her own opponent’s approach entirely, her blade lowering slightly as she traced the line of Rex’s shoulders.
She didn’t hear the junior guard’s sword whistling through the air until it was inches from her guard.
"Commander? Iris?" The boy called her name twice, his voice tinged with genuine alarm. "Commander, please! Are you with us?
Iris snapped back to reality as if she had been electrocuted. Her heart hammered against her bruised ribs.
"W-What?! H-huh... y-yeah... I’m here," she snapped, though her voice lacked its usual steel. "Focus on your footwork, not my face."
"Again!"

It was not new, exactly this magnetic, nauseating pull toward him. She had first noticed it days ago, a strange, unwelcome tightness in her chest when Sela had made an offhand comment about how unfairly good-looking he was.

At the time, Iris had dismissed it with practiced cruelty toward herself, telling herself it was merely grief finding strange, twisted places to leak out a phantom pain from a wound that refused to heal.
She had believed that lie and she had clung to it like a lifeline. She believed it considerably less now.
Now, she knew that the tightness wasn’t grief. It was something far more dangerous: recognition.
Her body recognized the predator, and despite the terror, despite the violation, there was a dark, shameful part of her that craved the attention of the storm.
The drills broke for a short rest as midmorning approached. Iris retreated to the edge of the hall, seeking the shadows to catch her breath and compose the fragments of her dignity.
Her lungs burned, and her hips throbbed with every shift of her weight.
That was when Diana arrived.

Diana swept across the training floor with the unhurried confidence of someone who owned the ground she walked on. She looked fresh, untouched by the morning’s sweat and steel, crossing directly toward Rex.
Iris watched through narrowed eyes as Rex turned when Diana reached him. Whatever correction he had been midway through delivering to the guards simply ceased.

He set the lesson aside without a second thought, his entire focus shifting as if the rest of the room had suddenly gone dark. In that moment, Rex was a man who had found his sun, and Diana was the only thing that mattered to him.

Rex leaned down, murmuring something to her too quietly for Iris to catch across the echoing hall, and Diana erupted into laughter. It was that specific, unguarded laugh she rarely granted anyone else, a sound of pure, unguarded delight.
Then, Rex did something that felt like a physical blow to Iris’s stomach: his hand came up to brush a stray strand of hair away from Diana’s face.
It was an absent, automatic gesture, but it carried more tenderness than most people managed in an entire lifetime of conversation. It was intimate and it was gentle.
It was everything Rex had refused to be to Iris.

Diana didn’t flinch. Instead, she leaned into his touch with the instinctive vulnerability of someone who trusted that hand completely, a hand that Iris knew could crush bones and claim souls with equal ease.
A bitter, acidic taste rose in Iris’s throat. The contrast was unbearable: the tenderness he showed Diana versus the brutal, possessive violence he had unleashed on Iris.
One received the sunlight; the other received the storm.
Iris couldn’t bear to watch any longer. She tore her gaze away, staring fixedly at the scuffed stone floor, feeling the familiar, hollow ache return to her center.
She forced herself to look away, tearing her eyes from the sight of them as if the image itself burned her retinas.
’I’m giving them privacy,’ she told herself, the lie tasting like copper and ash in her mouth. ’This is the decent thing to do...’
’Two people who care about each other, sharing a moment of quiet in the middle of this chaos...’
’I am being a good commander... I am being a good friend...’
But the words felt hollow, like echoes in a tomb. "Privacy" was a coward’s word for avoidance.
She wasn’t giving them privacy; she was fleeing from a mirror that showed her exactly what she lacked.

Desperate to ground herself, she busied her hands with a task that required none of her skill. She grabbed the leather wrap at her wrist, the one that was already snug, already perfect, and began to unlace it with unsteady fingers.
Her hands were shaking. She blamed the adrenaline from the drills, blamed the morning chill, and blamed the lingering soreness in her abdomen that made every breath feel like a transgression.
But deep down, she knew she was lying to herself again.

’Why does it hurt more than a blade wound?’ she wondered bitterly, her nails digging into the leather. ’Why does seeing him touch her feel like he’s reaching inside me and twisting what’s left of my heart?’
She focused on the ritual of the wrap, pulling the leather tight, tighter than necessary, until the pressure became a dull sting against her skin. She needed that sting.
She needed any physical sensation to drown out the psychological hemorrhage happening behind her ribs. She refused to look back.
She refused to acknowledge the way the sunlight caught Rex’s profile as he leaned toward Diana, or the way Diana’s eyes brightened.
She stayed anchored to her own small circle of pain, staring at the worn floorboards, counting the cracks in the stone as if they were a lifeline.
’Don’t look back, Iris...’
’Don’t give him the satisfaction of knowing you’re watching...’
’Don’t let him see how broken you are...’
She convinced herself that by ignoring them, she was winning. By turning her back, she was asserting her independence, re-establishing the boundary between her trauma and their happiness.
She convinced herself that if she could just keep her eyes fixed on her own hands, on her own equipment, on her own body, she could pretend the night before never happened.
She could pretend she wasn’t a woman who had been claimed and discarded, while Diana remained the woman who was cherished.
She convinced herself that she was fine.
But it did not help as much as she wanted it to.

The silence of the rest period felt heavier than the noise of the drills. Every muffled laugh from across the hall felt like a slap; every glimpse of Rex’s protective stance felt like a serrated blade sliding between her vertebrae.

The more she tried to compartmentalize the humiliation, the more it bled through the cracks. The more she tried to deny her own jealousy, that toxic, shameful cocktail of anger and longing, the more it poisoned her thoughts.

She was not giving them privacy. She was trapped in a prison of her own making, where every heartbeat was a reminder of what she had lost, and every second of silence was filled with the ghost of his touch.

chapters.title: Chapter 950. An Assassin Undone By A Hand On Someone Else’s Waist
paragraphs: By the time the training session finally wound down, Iris had constructed a fragile fortress of denial around herself. She had convinced herself that the morning had simply been an off day, the kind of ordinary, human lapse in performance that happened to every soldier eventually.
She told herself the dizziness, the distraction, the weakness—it was all just exhaustion, nothing more.

She nearly succeeded in believing her own lie. She almost made it out of the hall, her mind already shifting toward the practicalities of her next duty, until she took the shortcut past the training hall’s side entrance.
Then, the fortress crumbled.
There they were again. This time, there was no audience of recruits or guards to perform for.

The alcove was shadowed and secluded, bathed in a soft, amber light that seemed to isolate them from the rest of the world. Diana’s back was pressed against the rough stone wall, and Rex was close—impossibly close.
His forehead rested against hers in a gesture of such profound intimacy that Iris felt like she was trespassing on something sacred.
They were speaking in that low, private register, the kind of hushed murmur reserved for words that mattered less than the simple, shared oxygen between two people.
’Keep walking, Iris,’ her mind screamed, a desperate plea for survival. ’Turn around...’
’Walk away before you see something that kills what little is left of you...’
She should have kept walking. She should have retreated into the safety of her own solitude.
Instead, she stopped. Her boots felt like they had fused to the stone floor.

She hovered just past the edge of the doorway’s threshold, hidden in the shadows where neither of them would notice her presence. She was a ghost haunting her own life, watching a scene she had no right to witness.
She watched as Rex’s hand settled at Diana’s waist not with the bruising grip he had used on Iris but with a possessive gentleness that made Iris’s stomach twist.
She watched Diana’s fingers curl into the fabric of his shirt, seeking purchase, seeking connection. And then she watched the kiss.
It wasn’t a performance. There was no aggression in it, no demand for surrender.
It was an unhurried, simple act of wanting a quiet acknowledgment of each other’s existence. It was devastating.

Something in Iris’s chest twisted violently, a sharp, serrated blade of emotion that sliced through her carefully maintained composure. The pain wasn’t physical this time; it was something far more corrosive.
The pretense shattered completely, leaving only the raw, bleeding truth beneath.
She was jealous.

The realization didn’t come as a surprise; it came as a condemnation. She wasn’t just jealous of Diana; though the thought of Diana receiving Rex’s tenderness felt like swallowing broken glass, she was jealous of the certainty between them.

She was jealous of the way Rex looked at Diana as if she were his anchor, a stark contrast to how he had looked at Iris: as though she were merely prey to be broken, a vessel to be used and discarded.
’Why her?’ the question thundered in the silence of Iris’s mind. ’Why does she get the man who protects, while I get the monster who destroys?’

She was jealous of the ease of it all. She was jealous of the casual, constant physical affection that seemed to exist between them without either of them having to bleed for it, without having to barter their souls or endure the humiliation of a midnight violation.
Diana was wanted plainly, consistently, and safely. Diana was seen.
Iris stood frozen in the shadows, watching the two lovers, feeling the hollow ache in her own body intensify.
She realized then that she didn’t just want Rex’s touch; she wanted the version of him that Diana had, the version that didn’t leave her feeling like she had been gutted from the inside out.
She wanted to be wanted without being destroyed.

Iris turned away abruptly, her boots striking the stone with a hollow sound that seemed to echo too loudly in her own ears. She fled the alcove, her pulse hammering a frantic rhythm against her ribs, each beat a reminder of the vulnerability she had just exposed to herself.

She had not let herself want that simple, terrifying openness from anyone since Veylor died. In the raw, bleeding weeks following the funeral, when the grief had been so thick it felt like drowning, she had made a vow.
She had told herself that wanting connection again would be its own kind of betrayal, a desecration of the memory of what they had shared.
So, she had built it: a quiet, disciplined wall around that particular hunger, a fortress of solitude designed to keep desire at bay.
For years, she had mostly succeeded in not even noticing the wound was still there.
But watching Rex and Diana in that doorway, the wall did not feel disciplined anymore. It felt like a crumbling ruin, something she had been holding up out of habit rather than conviction.
The pressure of what she saw, the tenderness she craved and could never have, was cracking the foundation, letting the cold air of reality rush in to freeze her bones.
’Coward,’ she hissed at herself as she reached the main corridor. ’Pathetic...’
’You’re supposed to be a weapon, not some starving girl watching scraps fall from another’s table...’
She walked away before either of them could notice her presence, before Rex could turn his head and catch her fleeing like a thief in the night.
She spent the rest of the afternoon submerged in paperwork and equipment maintenance, telling herself, without much success, that the feeling would pass.
She convinced herself it was a temporary glitch, a momentary lapse in her emotional armor that would dissipate if she simply ignored it long enough.
It did not pass.
If anything, the ache sharpened over the following two days, transforming from a dull throb into a serrated edge that cut deeper with every passing hour.

Her senses had become hyperattuned to them, her mind involuntarily cataloging every minute display of affection between Rex and Diana, details she used to register with clinical indifference but now found impossible to ignore.
The torment was in the details.

It was the way Rex would find Diana at the end of every training session, without fail. He would cross the courtyard with that predator’s stride, and before a single word was exchanged between them, he would pull her in against him for one brief, grounding moment.
Iris would watch from across the yard, her jaw tightening until it hurt, feeling the phantom ache of her own body remembering the way his hands could grip her.
It was the way Diana would reach for his hand while they walked through the halls, an entirely unconscious, effortless gesture that neither of them seemed to think twice about.
It was so casual, so natural, that it made Iris feel like she was watching a foreign language she could never learn.
And then there was the quality of Rex’s attention. When Diana entered a room, Rex’s focus shifted like a compass needle finding north.

Even when he was speaking to a commander or instructing a recruit, his awareness remained anchored to her. His eyes would track her movement, his body would subtly angle toward her, a silent, constant tether that spoke of a devotion Iris had never dreamed possible.

Iris found herself trapped in a cycle of self-loathing. More than once, she would catch herself standing at the periphery of a room, frozen, watching the two of them share some ordinary moment of connection.

Her heart would race, her breathing would shallow, and she would have to physically jerk herself away, redirecting her attention to a map, a blade, or a weapon before someone noticed her staring like a starved animal.
’Stop it, Iris... Stop looking...’
’Stop wanting it...!’ The command echoed in her mind like a death sentence.

She was furious with herself, a cold, simmering anger that she directed inward because there was no one else to blame. She was angry in that specific, quiet way she was angry about most things she could not immediately fix through discipline, training, or violence.
Her entire adult life had been built on the bedrock of control: the control of her blade, the control of her mission, and most importantly, the control of her own desires.
She had trained herself never to want anything badly enough that its absence could be used as leverage against her.
And yet, here she was. An assassin with years of hard-won, lethal composure, utterly undone.
Her entire identity was fracturing, all because of the sight of a man’s hand resting at another woman’s waist.
